chapters.title: RCE Language Specification, draft 0.6: Overview
chapters.question: In the overview's tiny example, what is the name of the event?

sections.html:
Abstract. RCE is a small programming language whose programs mean one thing everywhere. A program is turned into a Form: a state machine given by its states, its events, a step function that maps a state and an event to a new state and an outcome, and the log of events. Every runtime that runs the Form must produce the same results bit for bit, and the rules that make this so are checked by machine.

Three plain points:

  1. Same answer on every target. Arithmetic, text, floats and concurrency have one defined meaning; there is no undefined behaviour.
  2. Every program ends. Loops, recursion and iterators are bounded, so the step function always returns.
  3. Memory is safe by construction. Ownership, second-class borrows, regions and linear handles rule out use-after-free and data races.

Tiny example (a counter that refuses to go negative):

RCE
state Counter
    n: i64 = 0
event Dec
step Counter on Dec
    check n > 0
    n -= 1

Status. Draft 0.6, 2026-10-13. Status: for review. Version 0.5 (sections 2 to 10) is unchanged from draft 0.5 except for the version declaration of 2.7 and rules W-VER-1, W-MOD-3 and W-TRAIT-3 now listed in section 7. Version 0.6 (Appendix C) is new in this draft: it is what the reference checker and the Lean files enforce and prove, and it applies only to modules that declare it, so every valid 0.5 program is still accepted. The core is mechanized in Lean 4 (spec/lean/, section 8), a reference type and well-formedness checker (spec/checker/, rce-check) implements sections 4, 5 and 7 including the admission gate of 6.9 (examples, checks, comptime and constants are evaluated), spec/tree-sitter/ is a tree-sitter port of the grammar checked against the LALR(1) tables of section 3, and grammar-level random programs are checked by rce-fuzz (spec/checker/). The production compiler has not been built from this document yet. Changes made while mechanizing are listed in 9.1 to 9.4. Draft 0.4 follows the language review in spec/LANGUAGE-REVIEW.md; draft 0.5 applies the changes that review proposed and draft 0.4 deferred (9.4).

RCE is defined by this document. A program is a text; its meaning is a Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) (section 6). Runtimes, emitters, harnesses and editors are not part of the language: they are implementations, and an implementation conforms when it accepts exactly the programs this document accepts and gives each one the meaning this document gives it.

Document status. This specification is the only normative text. SURFACE.md (the native surface design) and FORM.md (the compiler notes) are informative: two normative texts with two grammars could disagree, and only one of them is checked by machine. Their programs must still be accepted by the reference checker. The Form signature is 6.1.

The normative grammar is section 3, and it is also the machine-readable one: rce-spec-check (in spec/checker/, Rust only) reads the EBNF of section 3 from book/03-syntax.md, builds its LALR(1) tables and fails on any shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict, then parses every program in spec/examples/ and requires every program in spec/examples/reject/ to be refused, by the LALR(1) tables, the Rust parser and the tree-sitter port alike, then runs rce-check over the same files (all examples together form one program and must be accepted; the 12 syntax rejects, the 48 programs in spec/examples/ill_typed/ and the 16 in spec/examples/inadmissible/ must be refused). Current result (draft 0.5): 0 conflicts (100 rules, 472 productions, 932 states); grammar 51/51 accepted, 12/12 refused; checker 51/51 accepted, 12/12 and 64/64 refused (16 of them only by W-INT-1, W-CT-1 or W-LEX-3). Until 2026-10-12 the same grammar was kept as spec/rce.lark and checked with Lark (0 conflicts, 533 rules in Lark's expansion); that file is retired. rce-fuzz N SEED generates random type-directed programs from the grammar's productions, with targeted near-misses. 100,000-program run (8 parts × 12,500, seeds 1001–1008, spec/fuzz/RESULTS.md, with the former Python generator and Lark): all 100,000 parsed by LALR(1), exactly one Earley parse each, all accepted by rce-check; 516,012/516,012 rule near-misses and 392,362/392,362 syntax near-misses refused; 0 failures. That run used the draft 0.4 generator. From draft 0.5 the generator also covers extern, arena bound, structural recursion, f32, lane-wise arrays, device regions, byte text, u64, select, linear structs, LOOP_LIMIT and iterators; a 1,000-program run (seed 2026) of it has 0 failures. The Rust generator, with the section-3 LALR(1) tables as a third parser: 1,000 programs (seed 7), 0 failures, tree-sitter and LALR(1) agree on all 4,977 syntax mutants.

sections.html:
This section fixes how the rest of the spec is written and what it means for an implementation to follow it. EBNF (extended Backus-Naur form) is a notation for grammars; an inference rule states that a conclusion holds when its premises hold. For example Option = "[" Expression "]" . says an option is an expression in brackets.

Grammar notation. EBNF in the style of the Go specification:

Production  = name "=" Expression "." .
Expression  = Term { "|" Term } .
Term        = Factor { Factor } .
Factor      = name | token [ "…" token ] | Group | Option | Repetition .
Group       = "(" Expression ")" .
Option      = "[" Expression "]" .      (0 or 1)
Repetition  = "{" Expression "}" .      (0 or more)

Lower-case names are syntactic productions, UPPER names are tokens, and quoted strings are literal tokens. NEWLINE, INDENT and DEDENT are produced by the layout pass (2.6).

Judgment notation. Inference rules are written

Typing rules Name
premise1…premisenconclusion  [Name]\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\text{premise}₁\qquad …\qquad \text{premise}ₙ\end{array}}{\begin{array}{c}\text{conclusion}\end{array}}\;\textsf{[Name]}conclusion​premise1​…premisen​​​[Name]
Plain text of this block

Γ is a typing context (name ↦ type, mode), Δ a context of live borrows, Σ the declaration environment (types, kinds, traits, events, errors, regions). "iff" means if and only if.

Conformance. An implementation (a) refuses every text that is not in the language of section 3, or that breaks a rule of section 7, with a diagnostic naming the rule; (b) for every accepted program, computes δ, λ and the fold of section 6 exactly, including every edge in 6.3. Behavior the spec does not define does not exist: there is no "undefined behavior" and no "implementation-defined" result. The only implementation freedom is cost (time, memory, energy), never value.

chapters.title: 2. Lexical grammar
chapters.question: Which code point is the horizontal tab, as written in this section?

sections.html: This section says how source text is cut into tokens (the smallest meaningful pieces: names, numbers, keywords, punctuation) and how indentation becomes block structure. Getting this exact is what lets every tool read a file the same way. Example: let x = 0x1F # note is the tokens let, x, =, 0x1F; the comment is dropped.

sections.title: 2.1 Source text
sections.html: A source file is UTF-8 encoded Unicode text. A byte-order mark is refused. Line ends are LF or CR LF; a bare CR is refused. The horizontal tab U+0009 is refused anywhere in a file (layout is by spaces only, 2.6). A file that does not end in a line end is read as if it did.

sections.title: 2.2 Comments
sections.html: # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. A comment is part of the line end that follows it, so a line holding only a comment is blank for layout. There are no block comments. (# never occurs inside a token other than a string.)

sections.title: 2.3 Tokens
sections.html:
Tokens are identifiers, keywords, operators and punctuation, and literals. Spaces (U+0020) separate tokens and are otherwise ignored. Tokenization is maximal munch: at each point the longest token that matches is taken. Two consequences are stated so they are not surprises:

  • a<-b lexes as a, <-, b (a send), never as a < -b. Write a < -b.
  • t.0.1 lexes 0.1 as a float. Write (t.0).1.

sections.title: 2.4 Identifiers and keywords
sections.html:
Grammar NAME, letter, digit
NAME=letter { letter ∣ digit ∣ "_" } .(but not the single character "_")letter="A" … "Z" ∣ "a" … "z" ∣ "_" .digit="0" … "9" .\begin{array}{rcl}\textsf{NAME} & = & \texttt{letter}\ \{\ \texttt{letter}\ |\ \texttt{digit}\ |\ \texttt{"\_"}\ \}\ .\quad\textcolor{gray}{(\text{but}\ \text{not}\ \text{the}\ \text{single}\ \text{character}\ \texttt{"\_"})} \\ \textsf{letter} & = & \texttt{"A"}\ …\ \texttt{"Z"}\ |\ \texttt{"a"}\ …\ \texttt{"z"}\ |\ \texttt{"\_"}\ . \\ \textsf{digit} & = & \texttt{"0"}\ …\ \texttt{"9"}\ . \\\end{array}NAMEletterdigit​===​letter { letter ∣ digit ∣ "_" } .(but not the single character "_")"A" … "Z" ∣ "a" … "z" ∣ "_" ."0" … "9" .​
Plain text of this block
NAME = letter { letter | digit | "_" } .      (but not the single character "_")
letter = "A" … "Z" | "a" … "z" | "_" .
digit  = "0" … "9" .

Identifiers are ASCII. (Text values may hold any Unicode; names may not. This keeps names comparable byte for byte, which the name-free hashing of 6.6 relies on.) _ alone is the wildcard token.

Keywords are reserved and cannot be identifiers:

actor     after     and       arena     as        bound     break
chan      check     comptime  const     continue  default   device
elif      else      emit      error     event     example   extern
fail      false     fn        for       forall    from      if
impl      in        intent    iter      kind      let       linear
loop      match     module    mut       none      not       on
or        pass      pub       recv      refused   return    select
self      send      spawn     state     step      struct    then
to        trait     true      try       type      use       var
while     with      yield

device, iter, linear and yield are new in draft 0.5. lalr is not a keyword: drafts up to 0.4 reserved it in rce.lark and the tree-sitter scanner by mistake, without listing it here; draft 0.5 removes it from both.

catch is also a keyword. Keywords are reserved everywhere except as a member name directly after . (x.type, c.close()), where the grammar's member_name admits them; this is the only place a keyword can be a name (change S3). Note: class, unsafe, null, goto, async and await are not keywords; class and unsafe used as statements are syntax errors, and unsafe, Rc, Arc, RefCell as names are refused by rule W-SAFE-1 (section 7) so prototype code that used them is diagnosed clearly.

A \u{…} escape that is not a Unicode scalar value (a surrogate, or above U+10FFFF) is refused. - is never part of a numeric literal; -1 is negation applied to 1, except in patterns (3.9). true, false and none are keyword literals.

sections.title: 2.6 Layout
sections.html:
RCE uses indentation for blocks, as Python does, and the rule is the same one Python's tokenizer uses:

  1. Inside (…), […] and {…} line ends and indentation are ignored.
  2. Otherwise each line end that ends a non-blank line emits NEWLINE.
  3. The layout pass keeps a stack of indentation widths, initially [0]. On the first token of a logical line with indentation width w (number of leading spaces): if w > top, push w and emit INDENT; if w < top, pop while w < top and emit one DEDENT per pop, and w must then equal top (otherwise the text is refused: "inconsistent dedent"); if w = top, emit nothing.
  4. At end of file, emit NEWLINE if needed and one DEDENT per stack entry above 0.

Blank and comment-only lines produce no tokens. There is no line continuation character; open a bracket instead.

sections.title: 2.7 Language version
sections.html:
A module may declare its language version on its first line, as the comment

RCE
# rce-version: 0.6

The line must start with # in column 0 and hold, after optional spaces, rce-version: and a version; trailing spaces are allowed. The known versions are 0.5 and 0.6; any other is refused (W-VER-1). A module without the declaration is version 0.5. Version 0.5 is the language of sections 2 to 10. Version 0.6 adds Appendix C: its 23 words become keywords (C.1) and its constructs and rules apply. A version 0.5 module never sees Appendix C: its words are names there, and a valid 0.5 program is accepted unchanged by every conforming implementation. Because the declaration is a comment, the grammar of section 3 and its LALR(1) check are unchanged for 0.5; a 0.6 module is parsed by section 3 with the rules of C.2 applied, which is checked LALR(1) the same way. Each module of a program has its own version; a 0.6 module may use a 0.5 module and the reverse. (The reference checker has a non-normative conc06 build feature that reads undeclared modules as 0.6, for the draft's own test corpora; a declared version always wins.)

chapters.title: 3. Syntactic grammar
chapters.question: Which numbered resolution rule in 3.11 covers `send`? (for example R1)

sections.html:
This section is the complete grammar: which token sequences are programs. Its EBNF is read by the machine check (3.12) and checked to be LALR(1) (parsable left to right with one token of lookahead and no conflicts), so every program has exactly one parse. Example: fn half(x: u64) -> u64 = x / 2 is a function declaration with an arrow body.

The grammar is LALR(1) with no conflicts (checked, 3.12). Where a reader might see two parses, the grammar admits exactly one; the resolutions are listed in 3.11.

sections.title: 3.10 Statement and expression boundaries
sections.html: A Block always begins with NEWLINE INDENT, so a block can never be confused with an expression. A one-line form exists for the common cases: fn f(x: T) -> U = e, step S on E -> e, and Pattern -> stmt in match and select.

sections.title: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
sections.html:
Each is resolved in the grammar itself, so there is no precedence declaration and no conflict to resolve at parse time.

  • R1 dangling else. else only follows a Block (statement if) or is mandatory (if … then … else … expression). A statement if ends at its DEDENT, so the next else at the same indentation belongs to it.
  • R2 try … else against if … then … else. The branches of an if expression and the operands of try are CatchExpr, which cannot contain a bare try or if. if c then try a else b is a syntax error; write if c then (try a else b) else d.
  • R3 comparison chains. 0 < a < 10 is a syntax error (non-associative). Write a in 0..10.
  • R4 assignment against equality. = is a statement form, never an expression; (x = 1) is a syntax error.
  • R5 generic call against index. f[T](x) parses as index(f, T) then a call; name resolution (4.3) turns an index of a generic function or type by type arguments into instantiation, as in Go.
  • R6 impl generics against slice types. impl [T] … would be ambiguous with the slice type [T], so impl parameters need forall: impl forall[T: Show] Show for List[T].
  • R7 labels. In argument and pattern lists NAME ":" is always a label. Map literals {k: v} are in a different bracket, so {a: 1} is a map whose key is the variable a (write {"a": 1} for a text key).
  • R8 variant patterns against bindings. A Path pattern is a unit variant if name resolution finds a variant of that name in scope, otherwise it binds a fresh variable (Rust's rule). W-PAT-1 refuses a binding that shadows a variant name, so a misspelled variant is never silently a binding.
  • R9 send. <- after an expression at statement level is a send; in prefix position it is a receive. The two never meet: a <- <- b is "send the value received from b to a".

sections.title: 3.12 Machine check
sections.html:
rce-spec-check (in spec/checker/, Rust only):

  1. reads every rule of this section from its code blocks (the annotation column beside a rule is prose and is skipped), expands the EBNF the way Lark did ([ X ] and { X } inlined as with and without, { X } as one left-recursive helper rule), builds the LALR(1) tables and fails on any shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict (verified: adding | AddExpr "+" AddExpr to AddExpr makes it fail with 3 conflicts); current result: 100 rules, 472 productions, 932 states, 0 conflicts;
  2. parses the 51 programs in examples/, with and without their final newline; all must parse;
  3. parses the 12 programs in examples/reject/ (tab indent, chained comparison, if expression without else, try in a then branch, inconsistent dedent, class, assignment inside an expression, empty kind, state with no fields, step without on, example without ->, unterminated string); all must be refused.

Each program is parsed three ways (the LALR(1) tables on the reference lexer's tokens, the Rust parser, and the tree-sitter port) and all three must agree. Until 2026-10-12 this check was spec/check.py on spec/rce.lark with Lark in strict mode; both are retired.

spec/tree-sitter/ is the same grammar for tree-sitter (grammar.js, with layout, bracket depth, reserved-keyword NAME and longest-match numbers and <- in src/scanner.c). The former tree-sitter/compare.py N SEED parsed every example and N fuzz programs, each program's syntax mutants and SOUP lexical-stress mutants (a random token jammed in or a space deleted) with Lark and tree-sitter and required that both refuse, or both accept with identical trees (rule names, nesting, kept tokens and their text). chapters.title: 4. Programs, names and scope
chapters.question: What is the outermost scope called? (one word)

sections.html: This section says what a whole program is: a set of modules, the names each module can see, and the Form the program denotes. A module is one source file; scope is the region of text where a name can be used. Example: use std.text makes the module std.text visible as text.

sections.title: 4.1 Modules and packages
sections.html: A source file is a module. Its path is given by module a.b.c or, if absent, by its file path relative to the package root with / read as . and the .rce extension removed. use p.q makes module p.q visible under the name q; use p.q as r under r. Items are private to their module unless marked pub. Import cycles are refused (W-MOD-2). The modules std.text, std.collections and std.math are built in and always resolvable (S4); a program is the set of modules given together, and use must name one of them or a built-in module (W-NAME-1).

sections.title: 4.2 The program's Form
sections.html:
A Form module is a module (with what it imports) that declares at least one state, event or actor. The Form of the program is built from all Form modules reachable from the root (6.1). A module with only fn, types, const and impl is a library module: it has no Form of its own and denotes a set of pure functions.

A program whose root declares fn main() and no state is a command: it denotes the Form with one region Main of unit type, one event Start(args: List[text]), and δ given by running main (6.8).

sections.title: 4.3 Scope
sections.html:
Scopes nest: universe (built-in types and functions, 6.3–6.4) ⊃ package ⊃ module ⊃ item (generic parameters, parameters, state fields inside steps) ⊃ block. Declarations at module level are visible throughout the module regardless of order (so const N may follow its use). Inside a block a name is visible from its declaration to the end of the block. Shadowing a name from an enclosing block is allowed with let; shadowing a parameter, a state field or a module-level name in the same item is refused (W-NAME-2).

Namespaces: one namespace for values (variables, functions, consts, variants, events, errors) and one for types (types, kinds, traits, states, actors). Event, error and variant constructors live in both: as types (for patterns and payload typing) and as constructor functions.

chapters.title: 5. Static semantics
chapters.question: What is the name of the example kind used to illustrate error sets?

sections.html: This section gives the static semantics: the rules checked before a program runs. A type is the set of values an expression may have; ownership says which variable is responsible for a value, and a borrow is a temporary reference to it. Example: after let b = a where a is a List, using a again is refused because the list moved to b.

usize is a u64 used for lengths and indexes. f32 (draft 0.5) is computed in f64 and rounded once to f32 after each operation (6.3 N7), so every target gives the same bits. Float literals are f64; an f32 value is written x as f32, and f32 and f64 never mix without a cast. Box[τ] is List-like owned indirection of one element, needed only for recursive kinds; a &Box[τ] (or &mut Box[τ]) argument is accepted where &τ (&mut τ) is expected (deref coercion, draft 0.4). Every type has a kind of ownership (5.5): Copy, Move, or Borrow.

Integer ranges. An integer type denotes the mathematical integers in its range: iN = [−2^(N−1), 2^(N−1)−1], uN = [0, 2^N−1]. Arithmetic is checked against the declared type's range (6.3). Arithmetic on u64 and usize uses the Form's unsigned operations (6.3 N8, draft 0.5), so the whole range [0, 2^64) is available; drafts up to 0.4 trapped any u64 result at or above 2^63 (D7).

Text is byte-indexed (draft 0.5). s.len() is the number of UTF-8 bytes, s[i] is the byte at offset i as a u8, and s[a:b] is the text between byte offsets a and b, which must both be character boundaries (otherwise trap("not a char boundary")). Iterating for c in s still yields one-character texts. Go, Rust and Zig all index text by byte; the draft 0.4 code-point indexing made s[i] O(n).

Lane-wise arithmetic (draft 0.5). For arrays a, b : [τ; n] of one numeric τ and one comptime length n, a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b (and a % b for integers) apply the operator lane by lane and have type [τ; n]. Each lane follows the scalar rules (overflow and division by zero trap). Different lengths, or a non-numeric τ, are refused (W-SIMD-1). An implementation may use vector instructions; the result is defined by the lanes, so it is the same on every target. A list literal is a List unless it meets an array type of the same length, as an integer literal is i64 unless it meets another integer type.

Error sets. In τ ! ε, ε is a finite set of declared error names, written as one error name or as the name of a kind whose variants are all errors (type ParseErrs = … is not needed; declare kind ParseErrs with variants ParseFailed(at: u32) and Empty). Subtyping: τ ! ε₁ <: τ ! ε₂ iff ε₁ ⊆ ε₂, and τ <: τ ! ε (a plain value is a success).

sections.title: 5.2 Contexts and modes
sections.html:
A typing context Γ maps each variable to (τ, m) with mode m ∈ {let, var, field} and a liveness flag (live, moved). A step body runs in context step(R), a function body in fn, a comptime block in comptime, and an actor handler in actor(A). Effects are tied to the context:

A function called from a step does not inherit the step's effects; only the step body itself emits or sends. A function with a chan parameter is a task function: it may emit, send, receive, select and spawn, and it can be called (or spawned) only from main or another task function. Every other fn is a pure function of its arguments; a pure function, a step or a handler cannot call a task function (W-EFF-1). spawn f(ā) requires f to be a task function (W-SPAWN-1). (Change S2: draft 0.1 made every fn but main pure, which left nothing that spawn could start.)

Tail values. In a block-bodied function, if the last statement is an expression statement, or a match or if/else whose every branch ends in one (recursively), those expressions are the function's result and are typed against its return type ([Tail]; change S5). Elsewhere an expression statement's value is discarded, and an error union may not be discarded.

sections.title: 5.4 Types of declarations
sections.html:
• state R with fields fᵢ : τᵢ = eᵢ: every τᵢ is an owned value type (no borrows, no channels, no region types, no functions); every eᵢ is a comptime constant expression (W-STATE-2). R's type is the record {fᵢ : τᵢ}.
  • event E(fᵢ : τᵢ) and error E(fᵢ : τᵢ): payload types are data types: base types, tuples, arrays, List, Map, Set, options, structs and kinds built from data types. Events may additionally carry chan τ (a reply channel) when received by an actor.
  • step R on p if g -> e: in context step(R), the fields of R are bound as var, p is typed against the event sum, g : bool, and e must have the type of R's single field (only allowed when R has exactly one field; W-STEP-3). With a block body, the body is a statement list; the final state is the values of the field variables at the end of the block.
  • actor A with fields and handlers: like a state whose steps are the handlers, plus an address type A (a Copy handle) that supports a <- msg.

sections.title: 5.5 Ownership
sections.html:
Every value has exactly one owner: a variable, a field, a collection slot, a channel buffer, or the state. Types fall in three ownership kinds:

Copy   : bool, integers, f64, (), chan τ, actor handles, fn values,
         and tuples/arrays/structs/kinds all of whose components are Copy
         and whose size is fixed.
Move   : text, List, Map, Set, Box, options/tuples/structs/kinds containing a Move component.
Borrow : &τ, &mut τ, [τ] (slices exist only borrowed).

Rules:

  O1  Use of a Move variable moves it ([Var-Move]); a moved variable cannot be
      read, borrowed, or moved again until reassigned.
  O2  Assignment `x = e` to a var drops the old value of x first and makes
      x live.
  O3  `copy(e)` duplicates a value of any data type (deep copy); it is the
      only way to duplicate a Move value. (Copy-on-write is an
      implementation choice, not visible.)
  O4  At the end of each block, live owned values introduced in it are
      dropped in reverse order of introduction. Drop has no user-visible
      effect (there are no destructors), so drop order is unobservable.

sections.title: 5.6 Borrowing
sections.html:
RCE borrows are second class (as in Hylo and Swift's inout): a borrow can be created only as a function argument or as the operand of a for, a match, a method receiver, or a let whose scope ends before any conflicting use. A borrow cannot be stored in a field, a collection, a channel message, an event, a state, a closure that escapes, or be returned: with one exception: a function whose return type is a borrow (-> &[T]) must return a borrow derived from a parameter, and the result is tied to that parameter (R-RET). This removes lifetime annotations entirely.

Δ is a set of live borrows (ℓ, k, path) with k ∈ {shr, mut}. Paths are x, x.f, x[_] (any element), ordered by prefix (x ⊑ x.f).

A borrow ℓ ends at the end of the call or statement that created it (R-END), or for R-RET at the last use of the returned value. Because borrows never outlive the statement that made them except through R-RET, Δ is empty at every statement boundary not inside an R-RET region, which makes the check a local, linear pass.

Shared XOR mutable (theorem T6 relies on this): at every program point, for every path p, either Δ holds no mut borrow overlapping p, or it holds exactly one and no shared borrow overlapping p.

sections.html: This section continues the static rules for features that control where values live and what code may do: regions (arenas freed as a block), concurrency, traits, compile-time code, foreign functions, and the draft 0.5 linear types, device regions and iterators. Example: with arena r bound 4096 gives a block its own memory of at most 4096 canonical bytes, freed when the block ends.

sections.html:
with arena r introduces region r for the block. A type τ @r is allocated in r.

with arena r bound n gives r a capacity of n bytes (n : u64, evaluated once at block entry). Capacity is counted in canonical bytes, the length of the canonical JSON of each value allocated in r, so the limit is the same on every implementation. An allocation that would take r past n is trap("size limit"), and the event is refused as for any trap. Without bound the capacity is unlimited except by N9. The reference evaluator measures the values bound in the region after every statement of the region's body. So nothing allocated in r escapes the block; copying out (copy(x), or pushing a Copy element) is how results leave. Each step body runs inside an implicit region step freed when the step returns; state fields are not region-typed (they live in the state's own storage).

sections.title: 5.8 Concurrency
sections.html:
• chan[τ](n) creates a channel with capacity n (a comptime or runtime usize; 0 means rendezvous) and type chan τ; τ must be a data type or a chan. Channels are Copy handles.
  • c <- v moves v into the channel. <- c has type τ? (none when c is closed and empty).
  • spawn f(a₁…aₙ) requires every argument to be a data value or channel (not a borrow, not region-typed): arguments are moved into the task (W-SPAWN-1). Tasks share nothing but channels and actor handles, so data races cannot be written.
  • select arms: recv p from c (c : chan τ, p : τ?), send v to c, after n (n : u64 logical ticks), default. At most one default, at most one after.

sections.title: 5.9 Traits
sections.html: A trait declares associated types and function signatures. impl Tr for T must define every member with a signature equal to the trait's after substituting Self := T (W-TRAIT-1). Coherence: at most one impl of a trait for a type in the whole program, and an impl must be in the module of the trait or of the type (orphan rule, W-TRAIT-2). Generic functions are monomorphized (no dynamic dispatch, no vtables), so trait method calls are resolved statically. Built-in traits: Eq, Ord, Hash, Show, Copy, Data, derived structurally for every type whose components have them (f64 is Eq and Ord with the total order of 6.3, since NaN never exists).

sections.title: 5.10 Comptime
sections.html: An expression or block marked comptime, every const initializer, every array length, every state field initializer, and every argument for a comptime parameter is evaluated during compilation by the dynamic semantics of section 6 (with the same edge semantics). A comptime evaluation that traps or exceeds its fuel (6.7) is a compile error. A comptime fn may only be called at comptime. Comptime results become constants in the Form IR. Comptime evaluation cannot read files, clocks, environment or network (W-CT-1), so compilation is deterministic.

sections.title: 5.11 Foreign functions
sections.html:
extern "C" fn f(p₁: τ₁, …) -> σ declares a function implemented outside RCE with the platform C calling convention. It has no body. Rules (W-FFI-1):

  • The ABI string is "C". A foreign function is not comptime, not generic and has no self.
  • Each parameter type is bool, an integer type, f64, &text (passed as a pointer to UTF-8 bytes and a byte length), &[τ] or &mut [τ] with τ one of those scalars (pointer and element count). Borrows are second class (5.6), so the foreign callee holds them for the duration of the call only; no copy is made.
  • The result type is a scalar or (). No memory allocated by foreign code is ever owned by RCE, and no RCE allocation is freed by foreign code, so the two sides never need to agree on an allocator.
  • A foreign function may be called only from fn main and task functions (W-EFF-1), never from a pure function, a step, a handler or comptime, and it cannot be spawned (W-SPAWN-1). δ therefore never calls foreign code.
  • Each call is recorded in the log as Foreign(f, arguments, result). Replay supplies the recorded result instead of calling f, so the run of a command remains a function of its inputs and its log (T1, T3), with foreign results counted as inputs.
  • The memory behaviour of the foreign code is outside the language: T6 holds for the RCE side on the assumption that the callee touches only the buffers it was given, writes only through &mut buffers, and keeps no pointer after it returns. This is the trust boundary; it is named by the extern keyword at the one place it occurs.

sections.title: 5.12 Linear types (draft 0.5)
sections.html:
linear struct H declares a type whose values must be used exactly once. It is meant for handles to outside resources (a file, a socket, a device buffer) that must be released once and only once. Rules (W-LIN-1):

  • A linear value is moved, never copied: copy(h) is refused, and the type is not Copy whatever its fields are.
  • Every linear local, parameter included, is consumed (moved into a call, returned, or sent into a foreign function) exactly once on every path: a linear local still live at the end of its block, at return or at fail is refused, and so is one consumed on some branches of an if or match but not others.
  • A linear value is not moved inside a loop body unless it was created in that iteration.
  • A linear type may not appear inside a collection, an array, an option, a channel, a state or actor field, an event or error payload, a struct field or an iterator's element type. So no data structure can hide a second copy or drop one.
  • A foreign function (5.11) may take and return a linear struct whose one field is an integer or bool; the C side sees that scalar. This is how open/close pairs are typed.

Reading a field (h.fd) does not consume the value. Lean: RCE/Linear.lean (linear_exactly_once).

sections.title: 5.13 Device regions (draft 0.5)
sections.html: with device d [bound n] is a region (5.7) whose contents an implementation may place in accelerator memory. In addition to the arena rules, a device region holds fixed-size values only: no List, Map, Set, text, slice, channel or iterator may be bound in it, and its body may not emit, spawn, send, select, yield or call a foreign function (W-DEV-1). The body is therefore pure arithmetic on scalars, tuples, structs of those and arrays (with lane-wise operators), which is what accelerators run. Its meaning is the same as the block run on the CPU, so the region is only a placement hint; bound counts canonical bytes as for arenas.

sections.title: 5.14 Iterators (draft 0.5)
sections.html:
A function whose result type is iter τ is an iterator function. Its body is a block that produces values with yield e (e : τ) and ends by falling off the end or by return with no value. Rules (W-ITER-1):

  • An iterator function is pure (no chan parameter, no effects), and yield appears only in one.
  • A value of type iter τ may only be the operand of for or the receiver of .collect() (which returns List[τ]). It cannot be stored, passed or returned, so an iterator is never shared or resumed twice.

The meaning is the push model of Go 1.23 range-over-func: the loop body runs at each yield, break in the body stops the iterator, and return in the body returns from the enclosing function. The number of yields per run counts against the loop limit (6.7), so yield number LOOP_LIMIT + 1 is trap("loop bound"), and an iterator always terminates. Python generators and Rust iterators are pull-based and can be resumed from anywhere; the push form keeps delta total without any suspended state.

sections.title: 5.15 Standard library, effects and I/O
sections.html:
Standard library (normative). The standard library is closed: it is exactly the builtin methods below plus the concurrency methods of 5.8 and Appendix C (close, join, offer, put, wait, freeze, pscan, pscan_incl) and the num.rs primitives of 6.3. A method not in the table is W-NAME-1 at check time, so no program reaches an unknown method at run time. Every method in the table is pure and deterministic: it reads its receiver and arguments, and a method that "changes" a receiver (push, insert, sort, ...) updates only that receiver variable; none performs I/O. The table is checked against the reference evaluator (spec/checker/tests/stdlib_costs.rs).

Effects and I/O (normative). By derivation from least privilege, a program has no ambient authority: there is no file, clock, network, environment or randomness primitive. The only ways values enter are the events of E (6.1) and, in fn main and task functions, channel receives and foreign calls (5.11); the only ways values leave are emit (λ) and sends. Each of these is an effect of the context table above, so the checker, not run-time behaviour, decides which code may do I/O. Inputs that are not events (a select nondet choice, a foreign result) are logged, so replay is deterministic (T1, T21). A capability that is not in this list cannot be added by a library, because the library is closed.

Cost semantics. Each standard library call costs c_call plus the work of its complexity class on the sizes of its receiver and argument (C.6.4); see C.6 for the budget rules.

chapters.title: 6. Dynamic semantics: the mapping into the Form
chapters.question: Which JavaScript function is named for rounding to binary32?

sections.html: This section gives the dynamic semantics: what a program computes, as a mapping into the Form. It also lists the exact edge behaviour of every primitive (overflow, division by zero, float rounding, text indexing), which every implementation must reproduce. Example: -7 / 2 is -3, and i64.MIN / -1 traps with "integer overflow".

sections.title: 6.1 The Form of a program
sections.html:
Let the program declare regions R₁…Rₖ (state and actor declarations; actors also carry a mailbox), events E₁…Eₘ and errors X₁…Xⱼ. Its Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) is:

  • S = ⟦R₁⟧ × … × ⟦Rₖ⟧, where ⟦R⟧ is the set of records {fᵢ : ⟦τᵢ⟧} of R's field types, with the initial state s₀ = (r₁⁰, …, rₖ⁰), rᵢ⁰ the record of field initializers (evaluated at comptime). Actor regions add a mailbox queue and a held-message queue (Form law 3).
  • E = the disjoint union of the events' payload sets: E = ⊎ₗ {Eₗ} × ⟦payload(Eₗ)⟧, plus the built-in Tick(n: u64) and the task events of 6.8.
  • δ : S × E → S × O* (state and the outputs of the step) is defined in 6.4. It is a total function (T2).
  • λ maps each step to its output sequence O*: values emitted, and for a refused event the record Refused(X, payload).
  • D is the log: the sequence of admitted events e₁, e₂, …, each entry with its outcome (applied, or refused with X). The fold law: the state after the log is sₙ = foldl(δ₁, s₀, D) where δ₁ is the state component of δ.

Canonical signature (normative). This is the one signature; the engine profile (D.6), the engine IR (FormIr::step) and the language interpreter are instances of it, and any other text (FORM.md, papers) defers to it. S = Σc × Σd (control regions, data: regions, clock, input count, relations); δ : S × E → S × O* total; λ = π₂ ∘ δ; δ₁ = π₁ ∘ δ. An entry of D is the record {seq, event, prev_hash, state_hash, hash} where seq is the 0-based index, event is {type, payload}, prev_hash is the hash of the previous entry (64 zeros for the first), state_hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the state after the step, and hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash}. A log may also carry outcome, out and state; these are derived and must equal replay (T1), so they are not hashed. A refused event (T8) is recorded with its unchanged state and ends the example log. Both producers are tested against this rule (spec/checker/tests/form_signature.rs, tests/form_signature.rs).

Values ⟦τ⟧ are the Form's JSON-shaped values (form/types.rs): integers (i64), floats (finite f64), text, bool, null, lists, records. The embedding of RCE types into them is fixed:

Canonical order of values (used by Set, Map and select): null < bool < number < text < list < record; numbers by value; text by code point; lists and records lexicographically. This is a total order because NaN does not exist.

sections.title: 6.2 Evaluation
sections.html:
Expressions are evaluated by a big-step judgment ⟨e, ρ, σ⟩ ⇓ r, where ρ maps variables to values, σ is the store of vars and fields, and the result r is one of

  • ok(v, σ′): a value and updated store,
  • trap(m): a defined failure of the Form ("integer overflow", "division by zero", "non-finite result", "index out of range", "size limit", "loop bound", "value limit"),
  • fail(X, v): a user error raised by fail or propagated by try,
  • control signals ret(v), brk, cont (statements only).

Evaluation order is fixed: left to right, operands before operators, arguments before the call, receiver before arguments. and/or short-circuit. There is no other source of nondeterminism in expressions.

trap and fail propagate outward through every construct (they are not caught by catch: catch handles only declared errors and none; a trap always refuses the event).

&mut write-back (normative). A call writes back each &mut argument and a &mut self receiver on every outcome, including fail: the callee's writes made before it failed stay in the caller's store, exactly as an in-place update (fail above leaves the store at σ′, the store when it was raised, not σ). The derivation: the Rust target updates in place, and copy-in/copy-out agrees with in-place update only when it also copies out on failure (T33, WriteBack.t33; copyOk_differs shows that copying out only on success disagrees). Atomicity is per event, not per call: a trap, or a fail that leaves the step, refuses the event and the state is the pre-state (T8). The program emitters implement the rule for a write-back call that is a whole statement or expression of a let, var, assignment, emit or return, and for such a call under catch or try (f(&mut x) catch h, try f(&mut x)): the call is the first thing the statement evaluates, so it can be hoisted without changing evaluation order or budget charges. A write-back call nested deeper in a strict position (an operand of an operator, an argument, a list or map element, a receiver) is first rewritten by one shared A-normal-form pass that runs before all three emitters (spec/checker/src/anf.rs): the operands evaluated before it are bound to fresh let temporaries in left-to-right order, then the call, so reads, budget charges and emits keep their order (T34). A write-back call in a conditional position (right of and/or, an if branch, a catch handler, a lambda or a comprehension) is not flattened, since that would evaluate it eagerly; it is refused with a diagnostic, never given a different meaning. Tested on every target (spec/checker/tests/write_back.rs). Values of type τ ! ε are val(v) or err(X, v); they are first-class only until a try or catch consumes them.

sections.title: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
sections.html:
These are the Form's own rules; every implementation reproduces them exactly.

  • N1 Numbers. A Form number is an int (i64) or a float (finite f64). At every event boundary a payload is normalized: a finite float with no fractional part and |x| < 2^63 becomes the int (3.0 is 3, -0.0 is 0). RCE's static types make the int/float distinction visible to the programmer; normalization is applied only when values cross the Form boundary (event payloads, state, outputs) and is invisible inside a computation because each RCE value carries its static type.
  • N2 Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow of the static type's range is trap("integer overflow"), never a wrap. / truncates toward zero (-7 / 2 = -3); % has the sign of the dividend (-3 % 2 = -1). Division or remainder by zero is trap("division by zero"). Modular and clamped arithmetic are explicit methods, never the default: a.wrapping_add(b), wrapping_sub, wrapping_mul give the result modulo 2^N mapped into the static type's range, and saturating_add, saturating_sub, saturating_mul clamp it to the range; neither traps. u64 and usize arithmetic uses the Form ops uadd usub umul udiv urem (draft 0.5), which compute the exact result and trap unless it lies in [0, 2^64); a value at or above 2^63 is carried as an unsigned Form int, so 18446744073709551615 - 1 is exact. Lean: RCE/U64.lean. i64.MIN / -1 and i64.MIN % -1 are trap("integer overflow") (Rust's checked_rem). Shifts: x << n and x >> n with n ≥ bit width or n < 0 are trap("integer overflow"); >> is arithmetic for signed and logical for unsigned types. Bitwise & | ^ ~ act on the two's-complement representation of the static type.
  • N3 Floats. f64 operations are IEEE 754 binary64, round to nearest even. % is fmod (sign of the dividend). A non-finite result (±inf, NaN) is trap("non-finite result"): NaN and infinities never exist as values. x / 0.0 is trap("division by zero"). Canonical float text is the shortest round-trip digits; decimal notation for 1e-5 ≤ |x| < 1e16, else d.ddde±N with + on positive exponents (1e+300, 1.5e-7). f32 (draft 0.5). The Form ops f32add f32sub f32mul f32div round both operands to binary32, compute in binary64, and round the result to binary32 (round to nearest even). Binary64 has 53 ≥ 2·24 + 2 significand bits, so by Figueroa's theorem the result equals the correctly rounded binary32 result, and every target (Rust f32, Python struct, JavaScript Math.fround) gives the same bits. A result outside the binary32 range is trap("non-finite result"). x as f32 (Form tof32) rounds once. Lean: RCE/F32.lean.
  • N4 Mixed arithmetic does not exist in RCE (both operands of a binary operator have the same static type). a as f64 converts an integer exactly when |a| ≤ 2^53 and otherwise rounds to nearest even; x as iN truncates toward zero and traps if the result is out of range or x is not finite.
  • N5 min / max compare exactly on integers and by IEEE order on floats (total, since operands are finite).
  • N6 Equality is structural value equality after normalization; 1 == 1.0 is a type error in RCE (different static types), so the Form's "1 equals 1.0" rule matters only at the boundary.
  • N7 Text is a sequence of Unicode scalar values compared by code point, stored as UTF-8. From draft 0.5, len, indexing and slicing count UTF-8 bytes (Form blen, bget, bslice): s[i] is a u8, and a slice whose ends are not character boundaries is trap("not a char boundary"). for c in s and chars() still go by character. Case mapping (upper, lower) and class tests (isdigit, isalpha, isupper, islower) are ASCII-only; other characters are unchanged / false. strip and words split on ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \r, \x0b, \x0c).
  • N8 Indexing a[i] with i < 0 counts from the end (Python style); an index outside [−n, n) is trap("index out of range"). Slices a[i:j] clamp both ends into [0, n] and never trap.
  • N9 Limits. A list or text built by any operation is at most SIZE_LIMIT = 1,000,000 elements (trap("size limit")). A value written to state is at most VALUE_LIMIT = 1,048,576 bytes of canonical JSON (trap("value limit"), the event is refused, the value is not recorded).
  • N10 Absence. none and a present () differ, exactly as the Form's null-versus-absent rule: an option field holding none is present.
  • N11 Time is the logical clock only: Tick events and after n in select. No construct reads a wall clock.

The built-in methods on text and lists (len reverse sort sum min max upper lower strip chars words tostr toint abs all any unique flatten isdigit isalpha isupper islower get contains count index_of split join startswith endswith pow floordiv pmod zip replace append with map filter fold sort_by) have exactly the semantics of the Form primitive of the same name in num.rs and ir.rs (Prim, Map, Filter, Fold, SortBy), at the RCE static type. sort and sort_by are stable.

chapters.title: 6 (continued). Dynamic semantics: steps, loops and concurrency
chapters.question: Name-free hashing uses indices named after which logician? (two words)

sections.html: This section defines the step function δ (delta), which takes a state and an event and returns the next state and an outcome, then errors, hashing, loop bounds, concurrency and how examples are checked. A trap is a defined failure that refuses the event and leaves state unchanged. Example: a loop with bound 10 that starts an 11th iteration traps with "loop bound".

sections.title: 6.4 The step function δ
sections.html:
For event e = (Eₗ, v):

  1. For each region Rᵢ in declaration order, take the steps step Rᵢ on p if g in source order whose pattern p matches e and whose guard g evaluates to true in (Rᵢ's pre-state fields, bindings of p). The first such step is the step of Rᵢ for e. If there is none, Rᵢ is unchanged (frame). A guard that traps (overflow, division by zero, …) does not fall through to the next step: the event is refused with that trap (change S1; this is what makes δ a total function rather than leaving the case undefined).
  2. Every selected step runs on the pre-state s (ASM semantics, Form law 2): no step sees another region's update for the same event.
  3. The body of the step of Rᵢ is evaluated with fields of Rᵢ bound as vars to rᵢ, the pattern bindings as lets. Its result is
    • ok(σ′): rᵢ′ = the field values in σ′ (each checked against its type range and VALUE_LIMIT), outputs oᵢ = the values emitted, in order;
    • fail(X, w) or trap(m): the step is refused.
  4. If any selected step is refused, the whole event is refused: δ(s, e) = (s, [Refused(X or trap(m), e)]), where X is the refusal of the first refused region in declaration order. Atomicity: an event either applies to every region or to none.
  5. Otherwise δ(s, e) = ((r₁′, …, rₖ′), o₁ ++ … ++ oₖ).

The arrow form step R on p -> e is sugar for the block f = e where f is R's only field.

Order independence. Since each step reads only its own region and the event, the result of steps 2–5 does not depend on the order regions are evaluated except through "first refused region", which is fixed by declaration order. Outputs are concatenated in declaration order.

sections.title: 6.5 Errors, traps and refusals
sections.html: A fail X(…) or a trap inside a step refuses the event: the state is unchanged, the log records the event with outcome refused(X) and λ outputs Refused. Nothing is thrown past a step; no event is dropped silently. In a pure function called from comptime, refusal is a compile error. In main, a trap or unhandled failure ends the command with the refusal as its output.

sections.title: 6.6 Determinism of identity: name-free hashing
sections.html: Channel ids, actor ids and task ids are not counters. Each is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of (creating construct's name-free key, creating task id, per-task creation index), where the name-free key replaces identifiers by their De Bruijn position (Form law 2). Renaming every identifier in a program therefore leaves every id, every log hash and every select decision unchanged (T7).

sections.title: 6.7 Loops and fuel
sections.html:
for p in e iterates over a finite value (list, set, map in canonical order, text by scalar value, or an integer range a..b / a..=b); its length is fixed when the loop starts, and mutating the iterated collection inside the loop is refused statically (it is borrowed). while c bound n and loop bound n run at most n iterations, n a comptime-or-runtime u64 evaluated once; the default bound is LOOP_LIMIT = 1,000,000. A program may set its own default with a module-level const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n, n a positive literal (draft 0.5; any other declaration of that name is refused, W-LOOP-1). Starting iteration n + 1 is trap("loop bound"). Comptime evaluation uses the same bounds. for x in f(…) over an iterator function (5.14) counts yields against LOOP_LIMIT in the same way; Lean: RCE/Iter.lean (drive_total, drive_break).

Structural recursion (draft 0.4). A function may call itself when every self-call passes, in some parameter position i, a name bound inside a constructor pattern of a match whose scrutinee is parameter i (or a name already known to be such a component). The argument is then a strict component of the value received, so along any chain of calls the value at position i strictly shrinks and the depth of recursion is at most the number of constructor nodes in that value, which N9 bounds. A name that is rebound by let, var, assignment or a for pattern loses this status. Any other cycle in the call graph, including every mutual recursion, is refused (W-REC-1).

This is what makes δ total (T2): every construct terminates in a number of steps bounded by a function of the program and the event.

sections.title: 6.8 Concurrency: tasks, channels, select, actors
sections.html:
Concurrency is defined by a small-step semantics over configurations C = (T, K, A, L): a finite map T of tasks (id ↦ continuation), channels K (id ↦ capacity, FIFO buffer, closed flag, held-send queue), actors A (id ↦ region state, mailbox), and the log L.

Scheduling is a tick: tasks are ordered by id (6.6) and each runnable task takes exactly one communication step: it runs pure code until its next channel operation, spawn, select, emit or termination, and then performs that operation. All operations of a tick are staged and delivered after every task has moved (Form law 2: every update reads the pre-state). A tick is logged as Tick{n} plus one entry per communication action, with payloads (Form law 4).

  c has space                     ─→ v appended to c.buffer; task continues
  c full                          ─→ (c, v) held in c.held in arrival order;
                                     task blocked; Backpressure logged (no drop, law 3)
  <- c, buffer nonempty           ─→ first value; held send released in order
  <- c, empty and closed          ─→ none
  <- c, empty and open            ─→ task blocked
  spawn f(ā)                      ─→ new task id h(…); args moved in
  select: ready arms R ≠ ∅        ─→ execution k of this select statement in
                                     this task scans the arms cyclically from
                                     arm k mod n (n arms, source order) and
                                     takes the first ready one (draft 0.5)
  select: R = ∅, default present  ─→ default arm
  select: R = ∅, `after n`        ─→ blocked; after n ticks with R still ∅, after-arm

An actor is a region with a mailbox; a <- M(v) is an event M(v) admitted to a's region at the next tick; the actor runs its handlers by 6.4 with its own region as S. Each actor processes at most one message per tick, in mailbox order.

Fairness (draft 0.5). The counter k is per task and per select statement, starts at 0 and grows by one per execution. An arm that is ready at each of n consecutive executions of its select is taken by one of them (bounded wait). Draft 0.4 always took the minimal arm, so a busy first channel could starve the others, the problem Go solves with a random choice; the rotation gives the same guarantee without randomness. Lean: RCE/Select.lean (select_bounded_wait).

Because the order of every choice is a function of ids, payloads and per-select counters, and ids are content hashes, the entire run of a program is a function of its inputs: replaying the log reproduces it (T1, T3). The host may run tasks in parallel provided the observable result equals the tick semantics.

Deadlock: a tick in which no task can move and no input is pending ends the run with outcome Deadlock in λ (a defined outcome, not a hang).

sections.title: 6.9 Examples and checks
sections.html:
example ē -> o denotes the proposition: folding the events ē from s₀ gives a final step whose outcome is o, where for -> refused: X the last event is refused with X (earlier events must be applied), and for -> e the event list is fully applied and then

  • if the program has exactly one region with exactly one field f, the value of f equals ⟦e⟧;
  • otherwise e must be a bool expression over the final state, with fields in scope by name (or R.f when ambiguous), and must be true.

check e (in an intent or at comptime) is the proposition ⟦e⟧ = true, evaluated at comptime. A program is admitted only if every example and check holds (W-INT-1): the gate is part of the language, not of a test harness.

chapters.title: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
chapters.question: Which rule refuses two unguarded steps in one region whose patterns overlap?

sections.html:
This section is the checklist of rules a program must pass to be accepted (well-formedness). Each rule has a name such as W-TY-1, and a refused program is reported with the rule it broke. Example: a function declared -> i64 whose body returns text is refused by W-TY-1.

A program is refused if any rule fails. Every diagnostic names its rule.

Lexical and syntax

  • W-LEX-1 Not UTF-8, BOM, bare CR, or a tab character.
  • W-LEX-2 Inconsistent dedent (2.6).
  • W-LEX-3 A literal outside every possible type range, or an invalid \u{}.
  • W-SYN-1 Not in the language of section 3.
  • W-VER-1 A first-line # rce-version: declaration naming a version other than 0.5 or 0.6 (2.7).

Names and modules

  • W-NAME-1 Unresolved name, or a name resolved in the wrong namespace.
  • W-NAME-2 Duplicate declaration in one scope; shadowing a parameter, field or module-level name inside the same item.
  • W-MOD-1 use of a private item; W-MOD-2 import cycle. The reference checker reports a private name reached through use as W-VIS-1, which is the same rule.
  • W-MOD-3 An imported name that clashes with a declaration of the importing module or with a name imported from another module (imported names are not renamed).
  • W-SAFE-1 The identifiers unsafe, Rc, Arc, RefCell, transmute, static: refused with "memory safety is by construction" (there are no escape hatches in RCE other than the extern boundary of 5.11).
  • W-FFI-1 An extern declaration whose ABI is not "C", that is comptime or generic, or whose parameter or result types break 5.11.

Types

  • W-TY-1 Any typing rule of section 5 fails.
  • W-TY-2 Nested option τ??; borrow of a borrow &&τ; [τ] not behind a borrow; a borrow, region type or fn type inside a data type.
  • W-TY-3 Integer/float mixing without as; implicit narrowing.
  • W-PAT-1 A binding pattern whose name equals a variant in scope.
  • W-MATCH-1 A non-exhaustive match (5.3 [Match]); W-MATCH-2 an unreachable arm (subsumed by earlier unguarded arms).
  • W-PLACE Left side of an assignment or op= is not a mutable place.

Ownership and borrowing

  • W-OWN-1 Use after move (O1). W-OWN-2 Violating [No-Alias-Write] or [No-Mut-Read]. W-OWN-3 Storing, returning (except R-RET) or capturing a borrow. W-REG-1 A region-typed value escaping its with arena block.
  • W-SPAWN-1 Spawning with a borrow or region-typed argument.

The Form

  • W-STATE-1 A state with no fields; W-STATE-2 a field initializer that is not a comptime constant; W-STATE-3 a field type that is not an owned data type.
  • W-STEP-1 A step naming an undeclared region or matching an undeclared event. W-STEP-2 Totality: an event that no step and no actor handler can ever match. W-STEP-3 The arrow form on a region with more than one field. W-STEP-4 Within one region, two unguarded steps whose patterns overlap (the second is unreachable).
  • W-EFF-1 emit, spawn, channel operations or select in a pure fn; reading another region's fields in a step; calling a foreign function anywhere but fn main or a task function.
  • W-REC-1 A cycle in the call graph, including through trait methods after monomorphization, other than direct structural recursion (6.7).
  • W-CT-1 Comptime code that calls a non-comptime-safe function or traps or exceeds fuel.
  • W-INT-1 An example or check that does not hold.
  • W-SIMD-1 A lane-wise operator on arrays of different lengths, of an unfixed length, or with non-numeric lanes (5.1).
  • W-LIN-1 A linear value not consumed exactly once on every path, copied, moved inside a loop, or placed in a collection, field, payload, channel or iterator (5.12).
  • W-DEV-1 A growable value (List, Map, Set, text, slice, channel, iterator) bound in a device region, or emit, spawn, send, select, yield or a foreign call inside one (5.13).
  • W-ITER-1 An iterator function that is not pure or has an arrow body; yield outside an iterator function; an iter τ value used other than as a for operand or .collect() receiver (5.14).
  • W-LOOP-1 A LOOP_LIMIT declaration that is not const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n with a positive literal n (6.7).
  • W-TRAIT-1 An impl not matching its trait; W-TRAIT-2 incoherent or orphan impls; W-TRAIT-3 a type used with ==, !=, an ordering operator or a generic bound without implementing the trait it needs.

Version 0.6 only (Appendix C, applies only to a module declaring # rce-version: 0.6): W-PAR-1 to W-PAR-4, W-DL-1, W-ND-1, W-GRP-1 to W-GRP-3, W-SES-1 to W-SES-3, W-SCOPE-1, W-ATOM-1, W-ATOM-2, W-CRDT-1, W-LVAR-1, W-LVAR-2, W-NODE-1, W-SUP-1, W-SUP-2, W-INTR-1 and W-RT-1.

sections.html:
This section states the properties the language guarantees, such as determinism and termination, and records which are proved in Lean 4 (a proof assistant that checks proofs by machine). A theorem here is a statement about every well-formed program. Example: T8 (atomicity) says a refused event leaves the state exactly as it was.

Stated for well-formed programs (section 7). Proofs are mechanized in Lean 4 (v4.12.0, no Mathlib) in spec/lean/, over a core calculus: expressions (RCE/Expr.lean), statements, steps, regions, δ and the runtime fold (RCE/Form.lean), typing of steps and states (RCE/Typing.lean), an ownership core (RCE/Ownership.lean), the concurrency rules of 6.8 (RCE/Conc.lean), full borrow paths (RCE/Borrow.lean), the step bound (RCE/Bound.lean), name-free hashing and ids (RCE/NameFree.lean) and the Rust emitter (RCE/Emit.lean, printer RCE/EmitPrint.lean, differential harness emit-test/), structural recursion (RCE/Struct.lean, draft 0.4), and the draft 0.5 additions: select fairness (RCE/Select.lean), linear handles (RCE/Linear.lean), f32 (RCE/F32.lean), u64 arithmetic (RCE/U64.lean) and iterators (RCE/Iter.lean), and foreign replay (RCE/Replay.lean), &mut write-back (RCE/WriteBack.lean) and bound composition (RCE/Compose.lean).
