Most are proofs about abstract models (T18, T19b, T21, T22, T25 to T27, T29 to T31); T16, T17, T19a, T20 and T23 are proved on a small-step semantics of a core with par; none is a proof about the Rust reference evaluator.

T1 Determinism. For every program P, state s and event e there is exactly one (s′, o) with δ_P(s, e) = (s′, o). For a command, the full configuration sequence of 6.8 is a function of the input events. ∀ s e r₁ r₂. ⟨step P, s, e⟩ ⇓ r₁ ∧ ⟨step P, s, e⟩ ⇓ r₂ ⇒ r₁ = r₂.

T2 Totality of δ. For every s ∈ S and e ∈ E, evaluation of δ(s, e) terminates, and the number of evaluation steps is at most B(P) · (1 + size(s) + size(e)) for a bound B(P) computable from P (from loop bounds, SIZE_LIMIT and the call graph, which is acyclic except for structural self-calls; each of those contributes a factor bounded by the size of the value it recurses on, itself bounded by N9).

T3 Fold law. For every log D = e₁…eₙ, the state the runtime reaches is foldl(δ₁, s₀, D), and replaying D from s₀ reproduces every state hash and every output: ∀ D. run(P, D) = foldl(δ, s₀, D) componentwise.

T4 Progress. If ∅; Γ ⊢ e : τ and the store σ agrees with Γ, then ⟨e, ρ, σ⟩ steps, or e is a value, or e is a trap, fail, ret, brk or cont signal. (No stuck states other than defined outcomes.) For configurations of 6.8: either some task can move, or the run ends with a defined outcome (all tasks done, or Deadlock).

T5 Preservation. If Σ; Γ; Δ ⊢ e : τ ⊣ Γ′ and e → e′ (small-step presentation of 6.2), then there is Δ′ with Σ; Γ; Δ′ ⊢ e′ : τ ⊣ Γ′; and every value written to a state field of type τ is in ⟦τ⟧ (including its integer range).

T6 Memory safety. A well-typed program never reads a value after it has been dropped or moved, never observes a write through one path while another path to the same location is live (shared XOR mutable, 5.6), never reads a region after it is freed (5.7), and never shares mutable data between tasks (5.8). Formally: in the instrumented semantics that tags each location with an owner and a validity bit, no well-typed program reaches a configuration where an access touches an invalid location or two tasks hold a mutable path to one location. Foreign functions (5.11) are outside this statement: T6 holds for the RCE side under the 5.11 contract on the callee. (Approach: RustBelt-style semantic typing is not needed because borrows are second class; a syntactic progress/preservation proof over the instrumented semantics suffices.)

T7 Name independence. If P′ is P with identifiers consistently renamed, then every log hash, every id and every select choice of P′ equals that of P.

T8 Atomicity. If δ(s, e) refuses e, then δ₁(s, e) = s.

T9 Implementation agreement (per target). For every target t, ⟦compile_t(P)⟧ = δ_P on every s, e, including every edge of 6.3. There are two target sets, and a claim names its set. T9-F: the Form IR targets of the compiler (rce form --emit): Rust (native), WASM (the Rust crate on wasm32-wasip1), Python, XState and SCXML. T9-L: the program emitters of 10.5 (rce emit rust | python | js), which translate the checked module. A target outside these sets has no T9 claim. This is the theorem the differential tests sample; it is stated here so it is clear those tests check a property of implementations, not of the language. A differential test compares against the reference evaluator's trace, which the target under test does not produce.

T10 Grammar unambiguity. The grammar of section 3 is LALR(1) (checked mechanically, 3.12), hence unambiguous: every accepted text has exactly one parse tree. The same holds for the version 0.6 grammar (section 3 with Appendix C.2 applied), checked by the same machine.

T11 Select fairness (bounded wait). An arm of a select that is ready at each of n consecutive executions of that select (n arms) is taken by one of them.

T12 Linear use. In a well-formed program every value of a linear type is consumed exactly once on every execution path.

T13 f32 determinism. Every f32 operation gives the same binary32 result on every conforming target.

T14 u64 arithmetic. A u64 operation returns the exact mathematical result when it lies in [0, 2^64) and traps otherwise.

T15 Iterator termination. A for loop over an iterator, and .collect(), terminate after at most LOOP_LIMIT yields, and break observes a prefix of the values the iterator would produce.

T32 Foreign replay. For every oracle o answering foreign calls and select nondet choices (5.11, C.5), replaying the log of a live run reproduces its state, whatever o is; no property of the foreign code is assumed, and a contract every answer satisfies holds of every logged answer.

T33 &mut write-back. A call that writes back its &mut arguments on every outcome (6.2) gives the same store and outcome as updating them in place.

T34 Order-preserving A-normal form. Flattening an expression into let-bound steps in left-to-right order, with each temporary fresh, gives the same value, final store, and ordered trace of budget charges and emits as evaluating the expression.

Numbering and assurance. Theorem numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: a number is never reused or changed, new theorems take the next number (T32 on), and a split keeps its number with a letter (T19a, T19b). Code, tests, Lean doc comments and papers cite these numbers, so renumbering would break every citation for no gain in meaning. Each row's status uses one of the levels proved (Lean, on the RCE semantics or the named core), model (Lean, on an abstract model), checked (a machine check that is exhaustive for its input, such as LALR(1)), tested (sampled differential or property tests), in that order. A counterexample is a failure, never a lower level, and a claim about several parts has the lowest level among them. Every Lean name in the tables is checked to exist (spec/checker/tests/theorem_index.rs).

chapters.title: 9. Design decisions for review
chapters.question: The decisions list says it decides gaps in which file?

sections.html:
This section lists the design choices the spec makes, each with a one-line reason, and the changes made in each draft. Each decision can be reviewed and reversed on its own. Example: decision 45 makes text indexed by UTF-8 byte, as in Go, Rust and Zig.

Gaps in SURFACE.md that this spec decides. Each is one line of rationale; each can be reversed independently.

  1. Layout by indentation, spaces only, tabs refused (Python), with brackets suspending layout. Keeps SURFACE.md's look; tabs removed to make layout unambiguous.

  2. # comments only, matching the prototype; no block comments.

  3. Case-sensitive event names in examples. The prototype wrote example inc for event Inc; the spec requires Inc (no hidden case mapping).

  4. Several state regions per program, each step reading only its own region (pre-state, ASM), events atomic across regions. Matches Form law 2 and the "rules read their own sink" limit.

  5. Totality = every event is handled somewhere; unmatched regions are unchanged. Stricter than "every (region, event) pair", looser than "every event in every region"; catches typos without boilerplate.

  6. Errors refuse the event and leave state unchanged (example … -> refused: X), and are logged and output, never thrown.

  7. Traps (overflow, division by zero, non-finite, index, size, loop bound) are Form errors, not part of declared error sets; catch cannot hide them.

  8. Only structural recursion (revised in 0.4: a self-call must pass a constructor field of a matched parameter; mutual recursion refused) and every loop bounded (default 1,000,000, bound n to change), so δ is total by construction. Recursion on integers (f(n - 1)) is still refused; write it as a bounded loop.

  9. Second-class borrows, no lifetime syntax. Borrows only in parameters, receivers, loop/match operands and short lets, plus borrow returns tied to a parameter. Simpler than Rust, still no GC and no aliasing of mutable state.

  10. struct only, no class; value semantics, explicit copy() for deep duplication of non-Copy values.

  11. Integer types checked against their own range, all lowered to the Form's i64; u64 arithmetic results ≥ 2^63 trap. No implicit widening; no literal suffixes.

  12. f64 only (no f32), because the Form has one float.

  13. Bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons (unlike C/Python's & vs == in C), so x & 1 == 1 means what it reads as.

  14. if … then … else … as the expression conditional; no Python a if c else b (it collides with try … else).

  15. try e, try e else E, e catch d, e catch |x| h as the error vocabulary (Zig plus the prototype's else).

  16. Option is T? with some(x) / none.

  17. Generic arguments in square brackets (List[T], f[T](x)), Go-style, resolved by name resolution; impl parameters need forall.

  18. Argument labels Swift-style (fn move(from src: u8)), optional when the label equals the parameter name.

  19. comptime for consts, array lengths, state initializers, comptime parameters, and comptime blocks/expressions; comptime is pure and deterministic.

  20. Arenas are lexical (with arena r), region-typed values cannot escape; each step has an implicit per-step arena.

  21. Concurrency is deterministic by construction: ticks, staged delivery, content-hash ids, select chooses the least ready arm in canonical order, bounded channels with held sends and Backpressure logs (no silent drop), after n in logical ticks, Deadlock is a defined outcome.

  22. Pure functions cannot emit, spawn or use channels; only steps, handlers, main and task functions (those with a chan parameter) have effects (revised by S2).

  23. Actors are regions with mailboxes and handlers (on M(…)), one message per tick.

  24. A program with fn main and no state is a command: one event Start(args), outputs are its emits.

  25. Examples and checks are part of admission (the gate), and the outcome of a multi-field example is a boolean over the final state.

  26. Kind variants encode as {"$v": name, …} records in Form values; maps/sets as sorted lists, so canonical JSON hashing stays well-defined.

  27. Identifiers are ASCII; text values are full Unicode, case operations ASCII-only (as num.rs).

  28. No macros, no exceptions, no null, no inheritance, no operator overloading beyond traits Eq/Ord/Show: kept out to keep one meaning per text.

  29. Grammar artifact is Lark LALR(1) rather than tree-sitter: it is a deterministic LR table with mechanical conflict detection; a tree-sitter port is mechanical once the grammar is approved.

  30. Tail values in block-bodied functions (S5).

  31. A trapping guard refuses the event (S1).

  32. Keywords reserved everywhere except after . (S3).

  33. std.text, std.collections, std.math are built-in modules (S4).

  34. Loop elements of non-Copy type are borrows; storing one needs copy(x); lists, constructors, channels and vars cannot hold borrows (W-OWN-3, made explicit by the checker). Map get returns V ! Missing.

  35. Structural recursion admitted (R1). Bound: calls ≤ nodes of the value recursed on.

  36. C-ABI extern functions (R2): scalars and borrowed buffers in, scalars out, no allocator crosses the boundary, callable only from main and task functions, results logged for replay. Unwinding across the boundary does not exist because RCE has no unwinding.

  37. Arena capacity with arena r bound n in canonical bytes (R3).

  38. Explicit wrapping_* and saturating_* methods (R4); + - * stay checked in every build (there is no build profile that changes meaning).

  39. &Box[τ] coerces to &τ (R5).

  40. Effects stay inferred from context (5.2), with no effect annotations and no async/await; a task function is an ordinary function that has a channel parameter.

  41. Ownership stays affine, not linear, except for types declared linear (decision 46): ordinary values drop with no observable effect (O4).

  42. f32 computed in f64, rounded once (N3). Bit-identical on every target; the cost is one extra rounding instruction per operation.

  43. Lane-wise arithmetic on fixed arrays instead of a separate vector type; the array length is the lane count.

  44. Device regions are placement hints with CPU meaning; only fixed-size, effect-free code may run in them.

  45. Text indexed by UTF-8 byte, with character-boundary checks on slices.

  46. Linear structs for outside resources, consumed exactly once.

  47. Full-range u64 through dedicated unsigned Form ops.

  48. select rotates its starting arm per execution instead of choosing at random (Go) or always the least (draft 0.4).

  49. LOOP_LIMIT is a per-program constant with default 1,000,000.

  50. Push iterators (Go 1.23) rather than pull generators (Python, Rust): no suspended state, so δ stays total and replay needs nothing new.

sections.title: 9.1 Changes made while mechanizing (draft 0.1 → 0.2)
sections.html:
• S1 (6.4) A guard that traps refuses the event. Draft 0.1 did not say; δ was not total on that case.
  • S2 (5.2) Task functions. Draft 0.1 decision 22 made every function except main pure, so spawn f(…) could never be well-typed; a function with a chan parameter may now use effects and be spawned.
  • S3 (2.4) Keywords are reserved (the Lark grammar now uses a basic lexer, so the machine grammar agrees with the text), except as member names after .. Example 25 now uses labels source/target since from is a keyword.
  • S4 (4.1) Built-in standard modules, so use std.text resolves.
  • S5 (5.3) Tail values in block-bodied functions; examples 05, 06, 23 and 29 relied on this reading.
  • Examples were made whole programs: declared errors (18, 19, 22) and the emitted records (04, 31), defined report (07) and depth_shallow (29), added shop_pricing.rce for 26, parenthesized (try …) as u32 (07) and (m.get(w) catch 0) + 1 (21, which previously meant catch (0 + 1)), copy(i) in 16, and 08/09 declare their own trait Describe (the built-in Show cannot be re-declared or given an orphan impl).

sections.title: 9.2 Changes in draft 0.3
sections.html:
• The admission gate of 6.9 is implemented: rce-check evaluates every example and check, every comptime block and every constant and state initializer, and refuses a program on W-INT-1 or W-CT-1. W-LEX-3 (an integer literal outside its type's range) is checked.
  • rce.lark tree shapes (the language is unchanged): T? now yields an opt_type node, negative and true/false/none literal patterns, the three receiver forms (self, &self, &mut self), the two ends of a slice and e() versus e in example event lists are distinguishable in the tree. Draft 0.2 trees dropped these; found while porting to tree-sitter.

What the mechanized models simplify (stated so the coverage is clear): within a tick, sends are staged but receives consume in task-id order; select is modelled over channel ids only; actor state is a number; the borrow model's static context has the shape of the run-time state; H is an arbitrary function (no collision or SHA-256 model); concurrency is not evaluable at comptime.

sections.title: 9.3 Changes in draft 0.4 (from `spec/LANGUAGE-REVIEW.md`)
sections.html:
• R1 (6.7, W-REC-1) Structural self-recursion is admitted; mutual recursion and every other cycle stay refused. Checker: structural_violation. Lean: RCE/Struct.lean.
  • R2 (5.11, W-FFI-1, extern) A C-ABI foreign function interface: scalar and borrowed-buffer parameters, scalar results, callable only from main and task functions, results logged and replayed. extern is a new keyword.
  • R3 (5.7) with arena r bound n: an arena capacity in canonical bytes, exceeded by trap("size limit"). The checker types n as u64; the reference evaluator does not yet count arena bytes.
  • R4 (6.3 N2) wrapping_* and saturating_* integer methods; the default stays checked.
  • R5 (5.1) &Box[τ] coerces to &τ, which structural recursion over Box fields needs.

Draft 0.4 deferred the changes in 9.4 because each changes the Form or the emitters.

sections.title: 9.4 Changes in draft 0.5
sections.html:
• f32 (5.1, 6.3 N3): new type, Form ops f32add f32sub f32mul f32div and prim tof32 in form/num.rs, form_core.py and form_core.js. Lean: RCE/F32.lean.
  • Lane-wise array arithmetic (5.1, W-SIMD-1). It lowers to Form Map over the zipped lanes, so the Form needed no change.
  • Device regions (5.13, W-DEV-1, keyword device).
  • Byte-indexed text (5.1, 6.3 N7): Form prims blen, bget, bslice.
  • Full-range u64 (6.3 N2): Form ops uadd usub umul udiv urem. Lean: RCE/U64.lean.
  • select rotation and bounded wait (6.8). Lean: RCE/Select.lean.
  • Linear structs (5.12, W-LIN-1, keyword linear); extern may take and return linear structs with one scalar field. Lean: RCE/Linear.lean.
  • const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n (6.7, W-LOOP-1).
  • Iterators (5.14, W-ITER-1, keywords iter and yield). The reference evaluator runs the iterator with a yield cap, delivers values to the loop body, and re-runs with a doubled cap only when the body asks for more; gen_prefix shows this equals the push model. Lean: RCE/Iter.lean.
  • R3 completed: the reference evaluator counts arena and device bytes (canonical JSON of the values bound in the region, after every statement) and traps "size limit".
  • lalr is no longer reserved (2.4).
  • The four Form runtimes (Rust crate and WASM through num.rs, Python, JavaScript for XState and SCXML) agree on the new ops; the tests/form_num_v05.rs cross-runtime test compares them on about 6,600 cases.

Known open questions (not decided here): the standard library surface beyond the num.rs primitives; foreign interfaces other than the C ABI (WASM component model, GPU kernels); how an RCE module is used as a fit (the handler spec and fit formats themselves are now Appendix D); whether emitters should lower device regions and lane-wise operators to real accelerator or vector code (today they run them on the CPU, which 5.13 allows).

chapters.title: 10. Tooling: the `rce` command and the language server
chapters.question: Which JSON-RPC error code does the language server return for a request it does not know? (a number)

sections.html: This section defines the tools that read RCE programs: the rce command and the language server it contains. It adds no rules to the language; it says what each tool prints and returns for a given input. Example: rce run counter.rce "Inc, Dec, Dec" prints the state after each event and stops at the refused third event with exit status 1.

sections.title: 10.1 Principles
sections.html:
1. Determinism. Every subcommand is a function of its arguments and the bytes of the files it reads. Two runs on the same input give the same output bytes and the same exit status. No subcommand reads the clock, the network, environment variables or random numbers.
  2. No model in the loop. No subcommand and no language server request calls a language model, a remote service or any learned component. A diagnostic, a run, a test verdict, an emitted file and a formatted file come only from the rules of sections 2 to 7.
  3. One checker. rce check, rce test, rce run, rce emit and the language server all use the same parser, type checker and admission gate (6.9) as the reference checker rce-check. A file accepted by one is accepted by all.
  4. Exit status. 0 means success. 1 means a program was refused, an example or check failed, a run reached a refused event, or fmt --check found a file to change. 2 means a usage error: unknown subcommand, wrong number of arguments, unreadable file, or an unknown emit target or construct an emitter does not translate (10.5).

rce is one binary, built from the reference checker crate in spec/checker (crate rce-spec-check, cargo build --release --bin rce). The language commands of this section are implemented in spec/checker/src/cli.rs (entry point cli::main), with their tests in spec/checker/tests/. This rce carries the language commands only; the Form command line (rce form ...), which reads the Form spec format rather than RCE programs, is not part of this build, and rce form exits with status 2.

sections.title: 10.2 `rce check FILE...`
sections.html:
All FILEs form one program: use resolves among them (4.1). Each file is parsed, type checked (section 5) and admitted (6.9: every const, comptime block, check and example is evaluated). For each file, in the order given, one line is printed:

ok FILE
REFUSED FILE: line N: RULE message[; line M: RULE message ...]

Every refusal names its rule from section 7. Exit status 1 if any file is refused, else 0.

sections.title: 10.3 `rce run FILE [EVENTS]`
sections.html:
The file must pass rce check alone; otherwise one REFUSED line is printed and the status is 1.

With EVENTS. EVENTS is written exactly as the event list of an example line (3.2, EventRef { "," EventRef }), for example "Inc, Inc, Dec" or "Deposit(amount: 50), Withdraw(amount: 20)". Let s₀ be the initial state (6.1) and e₁ … eₙ the events. For k = 1 … n the command computes

(sₖ, oₖ) = δ(sₖ₋₁, eₖ)

where δ is the step function of 6.4 and oₖ is the sequence of values the step emitted (λ). It prints line 0 as 0 (initial) STATE, then for each k the line k EVENT STATE followed by one line emit VALUE per element of oₖ, in order. STATE lists every region as Region { field = value, ... }, regions separated by ; , in declaration order. If δ refuses eₖ, the line is k EVENT refused: ERROR, no later event is applied, and the status is

  1. Otherwise the status is 0. An event name that is not declared is a usage of a wrong event list: one REFUSED line, status 1.

For the counter spec/examples/01_counter.rce:

$ rce run 01_counter.rce "Inc, Inc, Dec, Dec, Dec"
0 (initial) Counter { n = 0 }
1 Inc Counter { n = 1 }
2 Inc Counter { n = 2 }
3 Dec Counter { n = 1 }
4 Dec Counter { n = 0 }
5 Dec refused: Underflow

Without EVENTS. The module must declare fn main() with no parameters. The command evaluates its body by the rules of section 6 and prints emit VALUE for each value emitted, in order. If the body traps or fails, the last line is refused: REASON and the status is 1. Calls to foreign functions (5.11) are not executed by the reference evaluator and trap. If there is no fn main(), the command says so and the status is 1.

The evaluator is the reference interpreter of the checker, with the fuel bound of 6.7 and the VALUE_LIMIT of 6.3. It is a definition of meaning, not a fast runtime.

sections.title: 10.4 `rce test FILE...`
sections.html:
The test cases of a module are its example lines and its check items, including those inside intent blocks. rce test admits the files as rce check does, which evaluates every case (6.9, W-INT-1). It prints, per file,

ok FILE (E examples, C checks)
FAIL FILE: line N: RULE message[; ...]

with E and C the numbers of cases in that file, then a total line P passed, F failed. Exit status 1 if F > 0. A test verdict therefore equals the admission verdict: a module whose examples do not hold is not a program (section 7).

sections.title: 10.5 `rce emit TARGET FILE`
sections.html:
TARGET names an output. The file must pass rce check on its own.

TARGETOutput
formthe Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) as one line of JSON (6.1), then a line end
rustone Rust 2024 source file with a main
pythonone Python 3 source file
jsone JavaScript module (ES2020 or later, BigInt) for Node

The Form JSON lists objects in canonical order (6.1), so it is a deterministic function of the program text.

The program emitters. rust, python and js translate the checked module, not the Form. Each output is self-contained. It starts with a runtime that defines the values of 6.3 and their operations, following the reference evaluator (spec/checker/src/interp.rs) value by value. That includes the integer range checks, the trap messages, map insertion order and the display of floats and text. After the runtime comes one target function per RCE function, method, step and constant. An expression becomes calls to runtime helpers with its operands in evaluation order; if, while, loop, for and match become the target's own control flow, with one counter per loop against its bound. Values are never changed in place: an assignment to a.f[i] rebuilds the value, as the reference evaluator's assign does.

The Rust output follows the shape of the verified emitter of T9 (spec/lean/RCE/Emit.lean): one value type, Result with ? for traps and refusals, and i128 arithmetic checked against each integer type's range. The theorem of T9 is about the Lean model of that emitter. The emitter in rce is tested against the reference evaluator; it is not proved.

What an emitted program does. Run it, and it prints the module's observations: one line per constant, per check, per function without parameters (other than main), per event of each example (the state after it, its outputs, or the refusal), and finally the outputs and result of fn main. These are the lines emit::observe computes with the reference evaluator, so that a target and the reference can be compared line for line.

How the emitters are tested. spec/checker/tests/emit.rs emits all 51 programs of spec/examples/ in all three targets. To exercise function bodies, it first adds probes: for each function and method, up to three calls on small sample arguments built from the parameter types, plus one example that sends every event. It then runs each output (rustc, python3, node) and requires its output to equal the reference evaluator's, line for line. All 51 agree on all three targets, with 299 observation lines per target. Four programs (14, 15, 34, 47) contain only concurrency and give no observation. A separate program (tests/emit_edge.rce) covers range traps, loop bounds, &mut write-back, closures and float display. When rustc, python3 or node is missing, its test prints SKIPPED and the reason; a skipped target is never counted as a pass. The oracles used were Python 3.13.5 and Node 20.19.2. The test reads the oracle paths from RCE_RUSTC, RCE_PYTHON and RCE_NODE (default rustc, python3, node on the path) and prints each oracle's version. On 2026-10-12 the same tests were also run on an Apple M5 Max (macOS 27.0.1, arm64) with rustc 1.98.1, Python 3.14.5 and Node 26.11.1: 51 of 51 agree on each of the three targets, 0 refused, 0 skipped, 299 observation lines per target, and the edge program agrees on all three.

Limits of the emitters.

  • Channels, spawn, select, actors and extern functions trap in the emitted code with the same message as in the reference evaluator ("not available at comptime"). There is no concurrent runtime.
  • The reference evaluator's fuel limit (50,000,000 steps) is not copied. An emitted program that runs longer keeps running, and deep recursion ends with the target's own stack error.
  • A call that writes back its receiver or a &mut argument (xs.push(x), f(&mut a)) is translated only as a whole statement or as the right side of let, var, an assignment, return, emit or fail. Elsewhere, rce emit refuses the program with status 2 and names the construct. No example program is refused.
  • When a function whose result is a union fails, its &mut arguments are not written back. The reference evaluator writes them back.
  • The Python output has been checked with Python 3.13.5 and 3.14.5, and the JavaScript output with Node 20.19.2 and 26.11.1. Other versions have not been run.

For an unknown target, or a program that one of these emitters does not translate, rce emit prints nothing on standard output, prints the reason on standard error, and exits with status 2. It never prints a partial file.

sections.title: 10.6 `rce fmt [--check] FILE...`
sections.html:
rce fmt rewrites each file into canonical layout. Let tok(t) be the token sequence of text t produced by the lexer and layout pass of 2.6, with line numbers dropped. The formatter is a function fmt on texts with:

  1. Meaning preserved. tok(fmt(t)) = tok(t). The formatter checks this equality on every file before writing it; if it would fail, the file is left unchanged, a REFUSED line is printed and the status is 1.
  2. Canonical layout. In fmt(t): a block that is k levels deep starts its lines with exactly 4k spaces; no line has trailing spaces; there are no blank lines before the first line, no two blank lines in a row, and the file ends with exactly one line end. A comment-only line takes the indentation of the next code line. A line that continues inside an open bracket keeps its position relative to the line that opened it.
  3. Idempotence. fmt(fmt(t)) = fmt(t). This is tested on every program in spec/examples/ and on the formatter's tests; it is not proved.

A text the lexer refuses (2.6, W-LEX-1, W-LEX-2) is refused by fmt with the same reason. fmt does not type check: a file that is refused by rce check can still be formatted. With --check, no file is written; each file that would change is printed as would reformat FILE and the status is 1. Without it, each changed file is written and printed as formatted FILE.

sections.title: 10.7 The language server: `rce lsp`
sections.html:
rce lsp speaks the Language Server Protocol 3.17 over standard input and output (JSON-RPC 2.0 messages framed by Content-Length headers). It keeps the full text of each open document; it does not read other files.

MessageBehaviour
initializereplies with capabilities: full-text sync (textDocumentSync = 1), formatting, hover, definition, document symbols, and completion triggered by .
textDocument/didOpen, didChangestores the text and publishes diagnostics for that document
textDocument/didCloseforgets the text and publishes an empty diagnostic list
textDocument/formattingreturns one edit replacing the whole text with fmt(t) (10.6), or no edit if t is canonical or refused
textDocument/hoverthe type or declaration of the name at the position, or null
textDocument/definitionthe location of that name's binding or item, or null
textDocument/completionthe names that can be written at the position
textDocument/documentSymbolthe document's items, each with its fields, variants or methods
shutdownreplies null
exitends the server: status 0 after shutdown, 1 without it
any other requesterror -32601, method not found

Diagnostics. For a document with text t, the published diagnostics are exactly the refusals rce check gives for t, one per refusal, with severity Error and source rce. A refusal line N: ... covers line N − 1 in the protocol's 0-based numbering, from column 0 to the start of the next line. use resolves among the module paths of all open documents.

Names. Hover, definition, completion and symbols all read one index of the document. The index is built from the parsed module and from the bindings the type checker declares while it checks the module: each local binding, with its line and its inferred type. A document that does not parse has an empty index, so these requests answer null or an empty list.

  • Hover on a local binding shows name: T, with the type T the checker inferred. On an item it shows the item's declaration: the line of a function, constant, event or alias, or the whole block of a kind, struct, state or trait. On a variant, field or method it shows that line.
  • Definition gives the line of the binding or item, and the column where the name appears on it.
  • Completion after . offers user methods, fields and the builtin methods of the reference evaluator. Elsewhere it offers the local bindings of the enclosing item, the module's items, variants and fields, and the keywords. Each list is filtered by the part of the name already typed.
  • Document symbols list the items in order, with fields of structs and states, variants of kinds and methods of impls as children.

Limits: the AST has no columns, so a name is found by scanning its line, and columns are counted in Unicode scalar values rather than the UTF-16 units of the protocol; the two counts differ only on a line with a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. A local is visible from its line to the end of its enclosing item: block scope is not tracked, so a binding of a closed block is still offered. Names are resolved within one document, not across use.

Because diagnostics come from the same checker, an editor shows a program as clean exactly when rce check accepts it (10.1, principle 3).

sections.title: 10.8 What is not yet implemented
sections.html:
• The program emitters do not run concurrency, actors or extern functions, and do not copy the fuel limit (10.5).
  • The language server resolves names within one document, without block scope, and counts columns in Unicode scalar values (10.7). It has no rename, references or semantic tokens.
  • rce run uses the reference interpreter; there is no compiled runtime.
  • Idempotence of fmt is tested, not proved.

This section lists the sources the spec draws on. It has no rules. Example: the f32 rule in 6.3 cites Figueroa, "When is double rounding innocuous?".

  • The Rust Reference, doc.rust-lang.org/reference; R. Jung et al., RustBelt, POPL 2018.
  • Zig Language Reference, ziglang.org/documentation/master (comptime, error unions).
  • The Swift Programming Language, docs.swift.org (argument labels, value types, actors).
  • D. Racordon et al., Implementation Strategies for Mutable Value Semantics, JOT 2022 (second-class references, Hylo).
  • Python Language Reference §2.1.8, Indentation (layout algorithm).
  • L. Maranget, Warnings for pattern matching, JFP 17(3), 2007 (exhaustiveness).
  • Y. Gurevich, Sequential Abstract State Machines Capture Sequential Algorithms, ACM TOCL 2000 (pre-state update semantics).
  • C. A. R. Hoare, Communicating Sequential Processes, CACM 1978.

  • Rust RFC 2945 ("C-unwind" ABI); The Rust Edition Guide, Rust 2024 (unsafe extern).

chapters.title: Appendix C. Draft 0.6 and 0.6b concurrency (normative for version 0.6 modules)
chapters.question: How many words does a version 0.6 module reserve in addition to the 0.5 keywords? (a number)

sections.html: This appendix defines the draft 0.6 language: structured parallelism (par, for ... par), budgets, deadlines, nondeterministic select and priorities (0.6), and the 0.6b extensions: workgroups, session types, structured spawn, cross-actor transactions, supervisors, nodes, interrupts, LVars and replicated state. It applies only to a module that declares # rce-version: 0.6 (2.7). A 0.5 module never sees any of it: its words are ordinary names there, and none of its rules apply. The text is written from what the reference checker (spec/checker, check.rs, check06b.rs, conc.rs, link.rs) and the Lean files (spec/lean/RCE/Par*.lean, Models06b.lean, Session*.lean, TickClock.lean, VClock.lean) actually enforce and prove; where the two differ from an intended design, the checker is what is described. Example: in a 0.6 module, par with two branches that write different variables gives the same result as running the branches in source order.

sections.title: C.1 Version and keywords
sections.html:
The 23 words below are reserved in a version 0.6 module, in addition to the 0.5 keywords of 2.4, except directly after . (so c.offer() and c.choose(L) remain method calls):

par       branch    nondet    budget    deadline  priority
replicated interrupt session  lvar      group     lanes
barrier   scope     atomic    protocol  offer     choose
node      supervisor strategy child     restart

In a 0.5 module they are names (fn f(node: i64) is valid 0.5). The reference checker keeps them in parse::DRAFT06_KEYWORDS, separate from parse::KEYWORDS, and reserves them only when the module is version 0.6.

sections.title: C.2 Grammar
sections.html:
These productions extend section 3 for version 0.6 modules. They are the productions of the tree-sitter port (spec/tree-sitter/grammar.js) and of the Rust parser. A rule below with the name of a section-3 rule replaces it for a 0.6 module; the others are new. The machine check of 3.12 also builds the LALR(1) tables of section 3 with these rules applied (lalr::book_grammar_06), lexing with the keywords of C.1 reserved, and fails on any conflict; it runs that machine over the 0.6 corpora (spec/conc06, spec/conc06b). So T10 (one parse per program) holds for version 0.6 modules too.

sections.title: C.3 Footprints
sections.html: The footprint of a statement is the set of place paths (5.6) it reads and the set it writes. Two branches are disjoint when no path written by one is a prefix of, or has as prefix, a path read or written by the other.

sections.title: C.4 `par`
sections.html:
par runs its branches; each branch is a block. The result equals running the branches in source order (C.4.2). Rules:

  • W-PAR-1: the footprints of two branches overlap (write/write or write/read), including through a &mut self method call.
  • W-PAR-2: a branch has an effect other than its own writes (emit, channel operations, spawn, foreign calls), or returns, breaks or continues out of the par.
  • W-NAME-2 also refuses two branches with one name.

sections.title: C.5 Budgets, deadlines and nondeterminism
sections.html:
• with budget n runs the block with a cost budget n: every Form operation charges its cost (C.6.4) and the operation that takes the total past n is trap("budget"), at the same operation on every target. The cost table is the reference evaluator's (interp and conc.rs, charge), listed in C.6.4. W-TY-1 if n is not an integer.
  • with deadline n runs the block with an expiry n logical ticks after entry; if the block has not completed by then, the else block runs instead (T22). W-DL-1: outside fn main or a task function.
  • select nondet may take any ready arm; the choice is an input and is logged, so replay reproduces it (T21). W-ND-1: outside fn main or a task function. select without nondet keeps the rotation rule of 6.8.
  • spawn f(...) priority p and event E priority p: admission prefers the highest pending priority (T25). W-TY-1 if p is not an integer.

sections.title: C.6 Cost semantics
sections.html:
C.6.1 A cost is a non-negative integer number of units. Cost is a deterministic accounting of Form operations, the same on every target; it is not a measurement of time or energy (est_j is separate).

C.6.2 Charging point. An operation charges its cost after its operands are evaluated and before it acts. If the charge would take any enclosing budget past its limit, the operation is trap("budget") and does not act; otherwise every enclosing budget is charged. So nested budgets see the same operation trap, and a budget n admits exactly the operations whose running total stays at most n.

C.6.3 par and for ... par charge c_fork per branch (or chunk), then each branch's own costs. The branches' costs are summed in source order, and exhaustion is placed where the sequential run would hit it (C.4.2), so the trap does not depend on scheduling.

C.6.4 The cost table (normative). Operations not listed (literals of scalars, variable reads, assignment, control flow, let) cost 0. The table is checked against the reference evaluator, and the emitted Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes charge the same costs (spec/checker/tests/stdlib_costs.rs).

OperationCost

standard library method (5.15) on receiver size n, first-argument size k4 + work(m, n, k), below

Method work (normative). A budget is a proxy for energy, and energy scales with the operations performed, so a method's cost must track its work. Sizes: text is its UTF-8 byte length, a list its length, a map its number of entries, any other value 0. n is the receiver's size and k the first argument's (0 when there is none). work(m, n, k) is fixed by the method's complexity class in the reference evaluator:

The calls a map, filter or fold makes to its function argument are charged as calls in addition (c_call each, plus their bodies). The arithmetic saturates at the largest i128, so it cannot overflow; no reachable size comes near it, so the Python and JavaScript runtimes, whose integers are unbounded, give the same numbers. work is monotone: it never decreases when n or k grows. The reference evaluator (conc::method_work) and the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes compute the same function, and the budget boundary falls on the same operation in all of them (spec/checker/tests/method_costs.rs, which also checks monotonicity).

sections.title: C.7 Device kernels
sections.html: Inside a device region (5.13), a version 0.6 module may use par and for ... par with the same rules; the device rules of W-DEV-1 still apply.

sections.title: C.8 `for ... par`
sections.html:
for x in e par runs the iterations as if in order. It is encoded in the reference checker as the marker region $forpar (the AST has no new variant). Rules:

  • W-PAR-3: the body writes a place other than as a reduction (+= *= &= |= ^= on a variable never read in the body) or as slot [i] of a range loop over i.
  • W-PAR-4: the body has an effect, or returns, breaks or continues.

A reduction is evaluated on a fixed tree, which equals the left fold for an associative operation with an identity (T18).

sections.title: C.11 Draft 0.6b
sections.html:
• C.11.2 Workgroups. with group g lanes n runs n lanes in phases separated by barrier. W-GRP-1: a group not directly inside a device region. W-GRP-2: barrier other than as a statement at the top level of a group body. W-GRP-3: a lane reads another lane's slot in the same phase, or lanes share a scalar written in the phase.
  • C.11.3 Sessions. protocol P declares a session type; a value of type session P is an endpoint. W-SES-1: an operation not allowed by the protocol state, an unknown label, offer() not matched over its labels, a match that does not handle every label, or branches leaving the endpoint in different states. W-SES-2: an endpoint not at the end of its protocol when it goes out of scope or is closed. W-SES-3: a label that appears twice, a protocol loop with no message before it repeats, or break outside a protocol loop. W-TY-1: a payload of the wrong type.
  • C.11.5 Merge. impl Merge for T declares a join. The admission gate (conc::crdt_gate) checks the merge laws (commutative, associative, idempotent) by evaluation on generated values; a failure is W-CRDT-1.
  • C.11.8 LVars. lvar T requires T: Merge (W-CRDT-1). W-LVAR-1: freeze() before the par or loop that puts to the LVar has joined. W-LVAR-2: wait with other than one threshold.
  • C.11.9 Structured spawn. spawn f(...) -> h gives a join handle. In a version 0.6 module a task function may spawn only inside scope; fn main is an implicit scope (W-SCOPE-1). A join handle cannot leave its scope (W-SCOPE-1). A 0.5 module keeps the rule of 5.8: any task function may spawn.
  • C.11.10 Transactions. atomic applies all its actor sends or none (T30). W-ATOM-1: spawn, a receive, select or another wait inside atomic. W-ATOM-2: actors of one atomic on different nodes.
  • C.11.11 Placement and supervision. node N {A, B} places actors on a node. W-NODE-1: a placed name that is not an actor, or an actor placed twice. supervisor S strategy k with k one of one_for_one, one_for_all, rest_for_one (W-SUP-1); each child must be an actor (W-SUP-2), and W-NAME-2 refuses a duplicate child.
  • C.11.12 Real time. interrupt event E priority p with p an integer literal in 0..=255 (W-INTR-1). step ... deadline n with n a positive integer literal in ticks, and const TICK_NS: u64 = n when declared (W-RT-1). TICK_NS only relates logical ticks to a nominal duration for reporting; no construct reads a wall clock (6.3 N11).
  • C.11.4 Replicated state. replicated state R is a region whose log is shared by replicas; a replica that applied a prefix of the log holds the fold of that prefix (T31).

sections.title: C.12 Rules that are not draft 0.6
sections.html: The reference checker also raises three rules that belong to the 0.5 language and are now listed in section 7: W-MOD-3 (an imported name that clashes with a declaration or with another import; names are not renamed), W-VIS-1 (use of a name private to its module, the form W-MOD-1 takes in link.rs) and W-TRAIT-3 (a type used with ==, < or a generic bound that does not implement the required trait).

sections.html:

"Model" means a Lean proof about an abstract model that is not connected to the RCE semantics or to the reference evaluator. "Vectors" means the reference evaluator's results on generated programs are checked against the model by the Lean kernel; that is a correspondence on samples, not a proof about the evaluator.

sections.title: C.14 Emitters and running
sections.html: rce run runs version 0.6 programs on the reference evaluator (conc.rs). The program emitters (emit/conc06.rs) run par branches in source order (C.4.2), which the meaning allows; a par whose branches wait on LVars is run by restart, and budgets charge the same costs as the evaluator, so trap("budget") falls on the same operation on every target. Workgroups run lane after lane per phase. The 0.6b actor, session and node constructs follow the limits of 10.5.

chapters.title: Appendix D. The engine profile: handler specs and fits (normative)
chapters.question: Which compiled node id does `deliverable D1` become? (for example role_R1)

sections.html:
This appendix defines the second input language of the engine: the handler spec, a line-oriented .rce file that rce check, rce compile, rce run, rce auto and rce form read (src/spec/parser.rs), and the JSON fit that says what each node of the compiled graph does (src/form/fit.rs). It is a profile tied to the language spec, not a second programming language: a handler spec declares a graph and its contracts; the behaviour of each node is a fit entry, and the compiled result is a Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) as in 6.1, with S, E and δ given by D.6. A file is a handler spec when its first non-blank, non-comment line starts with spec; otherwise it is a module of sections 2 to 10. Example:

spec "orders-form" v0.1.0
reason "Demo for the Form compiler" by "david"
currency max_age=24h

sections.title: D.1 Lexical rules
sections.html:
• The file is UTF-8 text read line by line. A line that is blank after trimming, or whose first non-space characters are # or //, is skipped.
  • A top-level line starts in column 0. A body line starts with a space or a tab and belongs to the nearest preceding top-level block. A blank line ends a body.
  • Tokens are separated by white space. A token that starts with " runs to the next " (no escapes); its value is the text between the quotes.
  • Durations: hours are N or Nh; milliseconds are Nms, Ns (seconds) or N. N is a decimal integer.

sections.title: D.3 Meaning of each declaration
sections.html:
• spec NAME VERSION: the name and version of the spec. The version is recorded in the compiled graph's metadata (spec_version) and in the Form IR (FormIr.version). The version is not yet checked.
  • reason WHY by AUTHOR: why an artifact exists. A top-level reason belongs to the spec; a body reason belongs to its block. A reason is recorded on the node or edge it explains and enters the log with every mutation that creates it. Reasons are data: they never change δ.
  • currency: when the spec's toolchain and dependencies were last verified (last_checked), the versions seen then, and the maximum age max_age in hours. Parsing is not a check: without last_checked the record is unchecked. rce currency FILE --mark records a check by writing last_checked back into the file. A record is stale when it was never checked or is older than max_age; the promotion gate records a stale spec, and blocks on it when the engine's enforce_currency policy is on (off by default).
  • objective, constraint, acceptance: requirements. Acceptance properties and their error budget feed the promotion gate; they do not change δ.
  • deliverable D compiles to the node del_D (an executor and a sink), role R to role_R (kind executor, decision, escalation or source), dependency P to dep_P (a source). flow F from A to B compiles to the edge flow_F; escalation E from A to B timeout t to esc_E. An endpoint names a node id, a node name or a declared id; an unknown flow endpoint is refused by the compiler, an unknown escalation endpoint is a diagnostic.
  • change_control: who may approve changes to the spec, the minimum review period, and whether the spec is frozen. These bind the engine's promotion path (spec mutations are logged and need an approver); they do not change δ.

sections.title: D.4 Fits
sections.html:
A fit is a JSON object:

{ "handlers": { NODE: HandlerSpec | {"kind": "term", "term": TERM}
                       | {"kind": "recorded", "contract": C, "table": {SHA256: RESULT}} },
  "types":    { SOURCE_NODE: TYPE },
  "keys":     { SINK_NODE: [COLUMN, ...] },
  "reads":    { SINK_NODE: {"key": [FIELD, ...], "into": FIELD} },
  "joins":    { SINK_NODE: [ {"relation": REL, "key": [FIELD, ...], "into": FIELD,
                              "scan": BOOL}, ... ] } }

An object with any of the five fields above is a full fit, even when it holds only reads or joins; any other object is a bare map of handlers and is read as handlers alone. NODE is a compiled node id (role_R1, dep_DEP1, del_D1). types gives the input contract of a source; keys the key of a sink's relation (default: the input number seq and the index n within the step). A recorded entry is an oracle: a recorded input replays its result and an unseen one escalates as "oracle miss".

sections.title: D.5 Reads, joins and scans
sections.html:
Each is applied before the body of every rule that writes the sink, to the state at the event's entry (pre-state, as in 6.4), in this order: the read, then the joins in list order.

  • reads[S] = {key, into}: the row of S's own relation whose key is the payload fields key (in key-column order) is put into the input as field into, or null when there is none. The relation must exist and its key must have as many columns as key names.
  • joins[S], an entry without scan: the row of relation relation keyed by the payload fields key, or null, into field into. The relation must exist and its key arity must match.
  • an entry with "scan": true: every row of relation as an array, in canonical key order (code point order of the canonical JSON key); key is ignored.
  • A payload that is not a record is passed unchanged. Joined rows and scans are typed as JSON. Each read or join is covered by the rule's SHA-256 id, and a rule with a read or a join is not monotone (CALM, form/laws.rs). A joins entry for a sink no rule writes is refused.
  • Every target (reference δ, Rust, Python, JavaScript for XState and SCXML) applies them identically.

CALM tags (normative). Each rule's monotone tag is derived by form::laws::calm_reason, never declared, and laws::check refuses an IR whose tag differs. A rule is monotone only when it has no resolve, no read, no join and no scan. The reasons, by derivation:

Rule hasTagWhy
none of the belowmonotoneits writes only add keys and grow counters
resolvenot monotoneit deletes escalation rows
readnot monotoneread-modify-write of its own sink
keyed joinnot monotonethe joined row may be null now and present later, or overwritten
scannot monotoneit observes the whole relation, so also what is absent

The tag is conservative (sound, not complete): a join against an insert-only relation would be monotone in principle, but the profile does not prove insert-only, so it is not claimed. A Form is coordination-free (laws::coordination_free) iff every rule is monotone. Because every read, join and scan sees the entry state, the post-state of an input event does not depend on the order in which rules for different sinks run; only the output order does, and that is fixed by content hash (law 2). Tested in tests/form_joins.rs.

sections.title: D.6 The compiled Form
sections.html: Σc has one region per node, Ready | Escalated. Σd has the logical clock, an input count and the typed relations of the sinks plus escalation and error. E is IN_<source>, TICK and RESOLVE_<node>. An input event normalizes the payload (6.3 N1), checks the source's contract (a mismatch is a reject output and an error row, not a refusal of the event) and runs the rules in content-hash order. A timeout is converted to ticks of a nominal 100 ms, rounded up; the clock is logical (6.3 N11). D is the canonical log of 6.1: entries {seq, event, prev_hash, state_hash, hash} chained by SHA-256. Every event is applied (no outcome field is needed), since a contract mismatch is an output, not a refusal. The numeric edges are those of 6.3, with one recorded difference: in this profile an integer above i64::MAX is "integer out of range" (D.10).

sections.title: D.7 Relation to the language
sections.html: A handler spec and a module of sections 2 to 10 both denote a Form, but the profile has no expressions of its own: node behaviour comes only from fits. A fit term is a term of the Form IR (form/ir.rs), not an RCE expression. How an RCE module is used as a fit is not yet defined (9, open questions).

sections.title: D.8 Lift guarantees (normative)
sections.html:
A brownfield lift (rce scan DIR --form, brownfield/lift.rs) reads existing Rust, Python, TypeScript or Go into a Form schema. Its guarantees are exactly these, each enforced by code and tests, and no other is claimed:

  • L1 Labeled: every relation, region, event and transition carries a label that starts with "unproven"; a lifted element is never presented as checked.
  • L2 Fail closed: a guard the lift cannot read is opaque, and Lifted::step refuses to step through it rather than guess.
  • L3 Generated code agrees with the lift: code emitted from a lifted machine (--emit-machine) steps as Lifted::step (tested, tests/lift_emit.rs).
  • L4 Evidence, not proof: agreement of the lift with the original program is tested on seeded runs of the original (tests/brownfield_lift.rs); its level is tested (8). A lift is an input to a gate, never an authority: what it proposes is admitted only through the checker and the gate, like any other proposal.

sections.title: D.9 Rules (normative)
sections.html:
These are checked by crate::spec::rules (src/spec/rules.rs), run by rce check, and each diagnostic names its rule.

  • W-HS-VER-1: the spec version is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH of decimal integers (an optional leading v is allowed).
  • W-HS-VER-2 (compatibility, between an old and a new revision of one spec, rce diff): the version must not decrease; a revision that removes or modifies a declaration must increase MAJOR, or MINOR when MAJOR is 0; a revision that only adds declarations must increase at least MINOR; a revision with no change may keep the version. Flows are declarations here: a flow whose endpoints change is modified.
  • W-HS-CUR-1: a max_age that is not a positive integer number of hours (N or Nh, N ≥ 1).
  • W-HS-CUR-2 (staleness): at check time now, the currency record is stale when it was never checked or now - last_checked exceeds max_age hours. A stale spec is refused by rce check --strict and by the promotion gate when the engine's enforce_currency policy is on; otherwise it is reported as a warning naming W-HS-CUR-2.
  • W-HS-REASON-1: the spec, or a declaration that compiles to a node or an edge (deliverable, role, dependency, flow, escalation), has no reason line, or a reason whose text is empty or unspecified.
  • W-HS-DUR-1: a duration that is not a decimal integer with an allowed suffix (D.1).
  • W-HS-KW-1: an unknown body keyword or change_control word.

sections.title: D.10 Recorded differences and open items
sections.html:
• Integers in [2^63, 2^64) are u64 values, as in the language (6.3 N2): the u64 operators compute on them exactly, comparisons, sort, lmin, lmax, min and max order them exactly, and the f64 and f32 operators convert them to f64. The signed operators refuse them ("integer out of range"), which no well-typed program reaches, since a signed value is never at or above 2^63. A JSON integer beyond u64 is read as a float (form::num); no integer type of the language holds one.
  • The cost model of extraction (est_j) and the gate's certificate are outside this appendix.

This file says how an AI agent shows that it has read the whole RCE spec, rather than claiming to. The spec is split into chapter files small enough to read whole. Each chapter ends with a footer holding the SHA-256 of its body and has one read-receipt question whose answer appears only in that chapter.

What the agent must do

  1. Read every file spec/book/NN-*.md listed in INDEX.md, in full, in order. Skimming, searching or reading a summary does not count.
  2. For each chapter, copy the hash from its last line (<!-- body-sha256: ... -->) and answer its Read receipt question from the chapter's text. Answers are short: a word, a name, a rule or a number.
  3. Report the result as JSON, one entry per chapter:
{"files": {
  "00-overview.md": {"sha256": "<64 hex digits>", "answer": "<answer>"},
  "01-notation.md": {"sha256": "...", "answer": "..."}
}}
  1. Say plainly which files were not read, if any. Never fill in a hash or an answer for a file that was not read.

How it is checked

rce-book verify receipt.json (in spec/checker: cargo run --release --bin rce-book -- verify receipt.json) recomputes each chapter's hash from the file on disk and compares each answer with a salted SHA-256 stored in receipts.json (the answers themselves are not stored anywhere). It prints PASS or FAIL per chapter and VERIFIED only when every chapter passes. Answers are compared after trimming, lower-casing and collapsing spaces.

A hash alone proves only that the agent opened the file; the answer shows it read the part that holds it. A correct receipt is evidence of reading, not of understanding. The salts are public, so a determined agent could guess short answers by hashing words from a chapter; doing that still requires having the chapter's text.

Keeping it valid

When a chapter changes, run rce-book build: it rewrites the footers, INDEX.md and spec/RCE-SPEC.md. rce-spec-check fails if the book and the single file are out of sync. If a change removes the text that answers a chapter's question, change the question and its salted answer in receipts.json in the same commit.

fn evens(n: u64) -> iter u64
